A structural order parameter, chi, ties the crossover into one non-equilibrium frame.
arxiv-2605-14364: Jiaqi Sun and colleagues propose MoRe, a framework for continual learning, learning new sequential data without erasing old knowledge. Rather than bolting modularity onto the architecture, MoRe finds modules inside the model's own form, in a hierarchy of fundamental and specific parts. The split comes with guarantees that modules can be told apart. Old modules stay intact by construction while new ones are reused, aligned or expanded during adaptation. Tests on synthetic benchmarks and real model activations show clear structure and a better plasticity-stability balance.
arxiv-2605-14664: Wang, Zou, Wu, Qu, Liu, Hu and Liu present MiVE, a framework for reference-guided video editing from a source video, a text instruction, plus a reference image. Separate encoders suffer modality gaps, while unified encoders lose fine spatial detail by using only final-layer features. MiVE instead draws on many layers of a vision-language model, since early layers hold spatial detail and deeper layers hold global meaning. It is claimed to rank first in human preference tests.
arxiv-2605-14864: Marina Godinho constructs new derived autoequivalences, symmetry-like transformations of derived categories, for Gorenstein orders. Given such an order and a quotient, she sets out conditions under which twisting around the restriction functor gives an autoequivalence. Along the way she shows the matching cotwist is a shift of the quotient's Nakayama functor. Local-to-global methods then yield fresh autoequivalences for skew group algebras and Hilbert schemes of group orbits.
arxiv-2605-15264: Kyle Finner and six others present the first near-infrared weak-lensing analysis of the Hubble CANDELS fields, spanning about a quarter square degree across five fields. High sensitivity to distant galaxies yields about 170 source systems per square sky patch. The analysis finds 12 shear-picked overdensities with masses from a fifth to just over twice ten to the fourteenth solar masses. Their redshifts run from about a fifth to just under one. Seven show diffuse X-ray emission consistent with collapsed structures, matching expected luminosity-mass scaling.
arxiv-2605-15364: Yuehui Xu and five others model detachment of cell clusters from Staphylococcus epidermidis biofilms, bacterial communities on medical devices that seed hospital infections. Old models reduce shedding to thickness or polymer density, skipping shed clusters' size and shape, which shape their biological fate. The new model weighs drag against adhesion in tagged biofilm sections set by cluster geometry and local germ-polymer layout. A tack knob sets polymer grip strength. Models checked to 24-hour biofilm data map how breakup changes shed clusters.
arxiv-2605-15464: Shangjian Yin, Yu Fu, Yue Dong, and Zhouxing Shi ask whether reinforcement learning from human feedback, learned from scratch in open-ended chat, can transfer to math and coding without domain-specific training. Their method, GRLO, trained on a small base model with only five thousand prompts, lifted average scores across domains from 24.1 to 63.1 while using far less data and compute than a strong in-domain baseline, and nearly matched much costlier released models.
arxiv-2605-15564: Minseo Kim, Huanghao Mai, Jay Shenoy, Alec Follmer, Gordon Wetzstein, and Frederic Poitevin present CrystalBoltz, a generative frame for protein crystal structure work. Measured diffraction strengths alone cannot fix a density map, since phases stay unseen. The frame casts refinement as Bayesian inference over atom layouts, steered by the measured strengths. It starts from a pretrained prior, samples with experiment guidance, then polishes atom spots and heat factors. It beats top rivals on spot error and fit, running 33 times faster than past experiment-guided refinement.
arxiv-2605-15664: Mayuko Kori builds a coalgebraic frame for non-wellfounded proof systems, whose global trace condition resists categorical account. Such systems impose a trace condition (GTC) on derivation trees for soundness. Kori models derivation trees as coalgebras of polynomial functors. Graphs of coalgebras then state the GTC as a condition on those graphs. Soundness becomes a unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism from a graph to an algebra. Within this frame, the GTC holds just when its adjoint image is recursive. Examples cover modal mu-calculus and higher-order fixed-point logics.
arxiv-2605-15864: Chufan Shi and six colleagues ask whether vision-language models that say 'let me check the figure again' look again. Their VisualSwap probe swaps the image for a different one after reasoning, then tests whether the model notices. On VS-Bench, 800 pairs from MathVista, MathVerse, MathVision and MMMU-Pro, Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL and ERNIE-VL miss the swap, with accuracy falling by up to 60 percent. Thinking models prove three times more vulnerable than instructed ones, and scaling offers no fix. User prompts restore grounding, but own reflections do not.
arxiv-2605-15964: Baining Zhao and fifteen colleagues propose WorldVLN, an autoregressive world action model for aerial navigation. Aerial navigation means following instructions through perception and action in 3D settings. WorldVLN adapts a video backbone to predict short world-state transitions and decode them into waypoint actions. Training grounds the video prior in navigation dynamics, then develops Action-aware GRPO, a reinforcement learning method for waypoint decisions. On outdoor and indoor benchmarks, WorldVLN beats baselines by over 12 percent in success rate, with larger advantages on hard cases, and transfers zero-shot to drones.
arxiv-2605-16064: Baek, Farias, and Wu ask whether simple algorithmic pricing can produce collusive-like prices in multi-firm markets. Firms using a myopic estimate-then-optimize rule fit demand to their own price and sales history, omitting rivals' prices. The authors characterize when this pipeline converges to prices above the Nash equilibrium, via a fluid-limit differential equation analysis. Supra-competitive prices arise when firms explore similar ranges on the same side of the Nash price, and can reach monopoly levels under symmetric exploration.
arxiv-2605-16264: Agrawal argues that push notification quality, how a message is composed, is an underinvested lever distinct from who, when, and what to send. He defines message quality along six dimensions, from contextual relevance and clarity to persuasive appropriateness, and shows language-model composition improves each over templates. Reviewed deployments report gains of 8 to 14.5 percent in click-through rate over static templates. He also warns gains are often misattributed to text alone, and offers a decision framework for when generation is the binding constraint.
arxiv-2605-16464: Tao, Wang, and Zhang propose Multi-Head Mamba, a U-shaped state-space model for 3D brain tumor segmentation. Brain tumors vary greatly in shape and multimodal contrast, making manual slice-by-slice drawing slow. The method splits the channel axis into state-space heads joined with skip links, improving long-range representation and multimodal training stability at linear complexity. A channel-space calibration module aligns statistics and boosts lesion response, while adaptive fusion at skip connections links global semantics to local details, improving boundary consistency.
arxiv-2605-16564: Chawla, Lee, and Shin develop PAM, a parallel mesh-free framework for discontinuous coefficient fields. PAM builds them as a continuous closed-form function built from radial basis functions. Shepard normalization steadies it near sharp interfaces, while sparse regression picks the best basis functions. Adaptive refinement adds detail where change is rapid. Theory shows this framework can approximate step functions to arbitrarily small error. Tests on Darcy flow, heterogeneous permeability fields, and the SPE10 benchmark show accuracy and scalability.
arxiv-2605-16664: Welc and colleagues describe building a fast, feature-rich development environment for Move, the smart-contract language of the Sui platform. Their strategy builds on the existing compiler core through the Language Server Protocol, rather than starting from scratch. They discuss alternatives they weighed and the optimizations needed as the language ecosystem grew. The paper closes with lessons for others supporting a fast-changing language.
arxiv-2605-16764: Huan and colleagues propose GDNet, a network for synthetic aperture radar image change detection. Conventional convolutional layers capture only local patterns and miss global context needed to distinguish subtle or large-scale changes. GDNet's global dynamic convolution module adapts kernel weights from global semantic information in the input, integrating local detail with long-range dependencies. A two-stage Mixup training strategy adds diverse samples and regularizes the model. On three SAR datasets, GDNet beats state-of-the-art methods, including under limited data.
arxiv-2605-17264: Deschênes and colleagues tackle robot mapping when violent tumbles saturate gyroscopes and corrupt lidar scans. They release the TIGS dataset, recordings of a lidar and inertial unit tumbling down a hill at angular speeds four times past prior sets. Two methods follow: one recovers true spin rates from saturated gyro data, and Stretch-ICP rebuilds smooth trajectories, cutting velocity errors at scan edges by about 95 percent.
arxiv-2605-17464: Li and Wang build a precise theory of observability loss and recovery for high-order discrete Galerkin methods for the multidimensional wave equation. Their spectrum analysis isolates one physical branch that regains continuous wave speed at low frequencies, while group velocity fades to zero at high-frequency symmetry points. Wave-packet building proves an exponential lower bound on the constant. A fix plan then brings back uniform observability for any fixed polynomial degree.
arxiv-2605-17564: Tseten Sherpa and colleagues explore a simple conditional U-Net for aerial RGB-to-thermal image translation, feeding weather data at the bottleneck within a Pix2Pix GAN setup with targeted pre- and post-processing. Trained on 612 paired images and tested on a held-out set, it reaches peak signal-to-noise ratio near 14.5, structural similarity near 0.81 and perceptual distance near 0.17, far ahead of the ThermalGen baseline. Conditioning data proves the most effective ingredient.
arxiv-2605-17664: Yunhui He and Leo Rebholz blend Anderson acceleration and GMRES, using Anderson's rule with true residuals. Both methods have boosted solver speed and toughness, each with advantages. The two differ in extrapolation, and Anderson uses fixed point errors while GMRES uses true residuals. Prompted by recent analyses, the authors apply the blend to Picard iteration for the Navier-Stokes equations. They provide convergence analysis and proof of speedup, a comparison of Anderson, GMRES and the blend, and an adaptive depth strategy.
arxiv-2605-18064: Taylan Yildiz and two colleagues study localization in a 1D quasiperiodic lattice extending the Aubry-André model with an Nth-neighbor hopping term. This tunneling couples windings of a helical chain and adds a control parameter. Working with noninteracting fermions at half filling, the team finds the delocalization transition using polarization. They compute polarization values of the Slater ground state and build a geometric Binder cumulant. The critical potential comes from the sign change of this cumulant, and stronger helical hopping holds the extended phase.
arxiv-2605-18464: Simone Carnemolla and four co-authors present PERL, a 2026 lightweight adaptation system that augments a frozen CLIP model. A compact shared reasoning module, applied in loops, generates a latent reasoning token at each step. The token enters an intermediate encoder layer, lifting higher-level meaning while keeping CLIP's pretrained structure. Across fifteen benchmarks it takes the best parameter-performance trade-off among compared methods, with only about 6K trainable parameters.
arxiv-2605-18564: Dibyendu Mahato and Wojciech Skomorowski derive, in a 2026 paper, short closed-form results for free-particle Green's function matrix entries over spherical Gaussian and plane-wave-modulated Gaussian bases. The proof uses Fourier transforms of Gaussians plus the addition rule of harmonic polynomials, giving fast recurrence rules. They also study long-range behavior key to low-energy continuum electrons in finite Gaussian bases. The results serve electron scattering and autoionization problems in quantum physics and chemistry.
arxiv-2605-18664: Karen Wadenpfuhl and five co-authors switch, with a pulsed terahertz field, the strength of interactions between Rydberg atoms by three orders of magnitude. Microwave fields can only reach states of similar principal quantum number, limiting how far interactions can be tuned. The team shows the switch through photon storage, where the terahertz field drives interaction-induced dephasing of the stored photon. Such fast switching aids single-qubit readout, state detection, quantum annealing, and Rydberg quantum optics. The work dates from 2026.
arxiv-2605-18764: Hyacinth Ali, Jessie Galasso-Carbonnel, and Houari Sahraoui present DDAP, a 2026 guided framework helping non-experts to build AI pipelines. Many lack the expertise to design AI systems, though pipelines now serve medicine, agriculture, and social science. DDAP runs four stages: problem scope, environment setup, pipeline building, and code building. It adapts to domain context, user skill, and resource limits while keeping user control. Tested across business, biology, and health data against expert models, DDAP reaches competitive results in several tasks, though performance varies for text clustering.
arxiv-2605-18864: Chanuk Lee, Minki Kang and Sung Ju Hwang ask why reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards sharpens a language model's best answer but rarely widens its reasoning paths. They trace the limit to reverse-KL regularization, which anchors training to a reference model and suppresses new modes of thought. Dropping or swapping that penalty creates reward hacking or wasted probability. Their SAGE framework instead reshapes the anchor itself through a guide function, and tests on hard mathematics benchmarks show gains in both single-answer accuracy and broader coverage.
arxiv-2605-19164: Marco Mandap builds a Cramér-von Mises test for complete spatial randomness that does not depend on origin placement. It averages corner gaps between observed and uniform patterns over all cube corners, with a fast closed-form formula. In one dimension it matches the classic rank test; in two it matches Zimmerman's origin-invariant form. Under random placement, the process tends to a centered Gaussian process with explicit cross-corner covariance. Monte Carlo runs show sound calibration and sensitivity against fixed non-uniform alternatives.
arxiv-2605-19464: Arutkin and Vallée ask how fluctuating volatility picks the Pareto tail of wealth in random growth with redistribution. The Bouchaud-Mézard model gives stationary Pareto tails but fixes noise intensity, an awkward limit for real growth where volatility moves. Replacing fixed intensity with switching diffusivity, they show the long-time Gaussian limit holds when the redraw law has finite mean and variance, with persistence adding to asymptotic variance. For two-state diffusivity an exact tail analysis yields a Pareto exponent sliding between slow-refresh and fast-refresh limits.
arxiv-2605-19664: Mędrzycka and team build tunable Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains in liquid crystal microcavities. They emulate topological phases hard to realize in plain matter, and liquid crystal versions add room-temperature tuning through voltage-set splitting, spin-orbit coupling and self-grown patterns. The authors design a cavity hosting a paired uniform lying helix texture, whose light potential gives two coupled SSH chains with crossed polarizations acting as a pseudospin. Applied voltage tunes the inter-chain coupling, giving polarization-tuned effects and making these cavities a platform for tunable Hamiltonians.
arxiv-2605-19964: Tatsuya Wada and three co-workers study Lee-Yang zeros, the complex points where a finite system's partition function vanishes, in a mean-field model of quantum chromodynamics. They track how the zeros and the related edge singularity move with temperature and system size. When they compare critical-point methods based on finite-size scaling of zeros and susceptibility ratios, they find careful handling of corrections from irrelevant operators is key for accuracy.
arxiv-2605-21064: Vladimir Dzhunushaliev and V. Folomeev consider arguments for a fermion condensate at the event horizon. They argue that canonical anticommutation relations for fermions should be changed in curved spacetime near a black hole event horizon. Such a change is expected to alter the source term of the inhomogeneous Dirac equation for the two-point Green's function. By adding an ad hoc source into the Dirac formula that mimics those relations, they obtain stationary solutions read as two-point Green's functions of fermions near the horizon.
arxiv-2605-21164: Adam Innan and colleagues tackle credit-card fraud detection, where rare fraud cases skew models toward the common legitimate class. Their Q-SYNTH system pairs a quantum circuit generator with a classical neural network discriminator to create synthetic fraud samples for tabular data. Samples are judged on statistical fidelity, on how hard they are to tell from real fraud, and on downstream detection gains. Under their protocol, Q-SYNTH cut distribution mismatch against real fraud.
arxiv-2605-21364: Nirbhay Patil, Ada Altieri, and Fabián Aguirre-López derive a method to apply dynamical mean-field theory to ultra small-world networks. Social, economic, and ecological networks often show inter-nodal distance growing even slower than logarithmically with system size, yet theory often assumes systems outside this regime. Their method accounts for degree correlations arising from network constraints, known as structural cut-offs, in highly heterogeneous networks. Applied to the disordered Lotka-Volterra model, it matches simulated and empirically sourced networks far better.
arxiv-2605-21564: Sneha Pradhan's thesis studies compact astrophysical objects in modified theories of gravity, on neutron stars and strange stars. She builds charged even compact star models in f(Q) gravity with conformal symmetry and the MIT Bag rule of state, matched to a Bardeen outside. Decoupling methods in f(T) gravity yield anisotropic strange star models, adding extra sources, dark matter effects, and spacetime deformations. Checks use energy conditions, causality limits, and Herrera's cracking criterion, and a Bayesian framework constrains values with NICER mass-radius data.
arxiv-2605-21764: Tran proves quasi-optimal and lower-order error estimates for weak Galerkin, discontinuous Galerkin, and hybrid-high-order finite element methods for the biharmonic equation. The estimates hold under minimal smoothness assumptions on general polytopal meshes. The paper also shows that stabilization helps a posteriori error estimators. These three method types thus gain a shared error analysis on general meshes.
arxiv-2605-22364: Zvizdenco and colleagues scale up solving for the Optimal Observability Problem. The task is to pick what sensing an agent should use when the world is not known. Success must be weighed against kit and compute costs. Past work cast the task with Markov decision processes. The team looks at two solvable parts, sensor choice and positional observability. A new method finds good sensing rules by splitting decision processes. It lifts instance size by 3 orders of magnitude and run time by 5.
arxiv-2605-22564: Wang and team launch SynAE, testing how well fake benchmarks for tool agents copy and augment real data paths. Tool agents are tested on static run traces, but in-house sets are sparse. Teams more and more use fake sets, raising the problem of sizing the fake-real link. SynAE tests truth, match, and range: prompts and replies; tool calls; final outputs; and downstream tests. On recent benchmarks, SynAE detects shifts in truth, match, range. It shows no single metric covers fake data quality, driving multi-axis checks.
arxiv-2605-22664: Yen and others evaluate language model agents on end to end spreadsheet work in finance, a skill prior benchmarks missed by testing only question answering or single formula edits. Their MBABench set grades full deliverables on accuracy, formula quality and format, reflecting professional review standards for modelling, forecasting and scenario analysis. Across 18 agents, even the strongest fall short of basic professional standards, and scores drop sharply once tasks chain beyond a few calculations. The authors conclude current agents cannot yet reliably produce professional grade spreadsheets at real world complexity.
arxiv-2605-22864: Eusebi and five colleagues read calibrated uncertainty from the path a language model's representation takes through its layers, not just its final probabilities. They trace eleven scale-invariant geometric features of cumulative MLP updates and feed these to a sparse linear probe. The probe beat the standard maximum-probability baseline under selective abstention, gaining up to 21 points where miscalibration was worst. Its coefficients show which layers commit too early or drift from the endpoint.
arxiv-2605-22964: Back de Luca and Fountoulakis show that certifying a learned guess from examples turns vastly hard under minimal overparametrization. For threshold circuits of depth at least two, one extra gate can force certificate sizes that grow exponentially with input size. Log-precision Transformers show a similar barrier with only constant overhead. Even allowing polynomially many mistakes still demands huge certificates. Yet constant error guarantees can hide vastly many mistakes. Tests on binary addition circuits and trained Transformers confirm the barrier.
arxiv-2605-23164: Kleman and three coauthors urge caution in reading group gaps in genetic risk. Trait values across human groups attract renewed interest with gene studies and polygenic risk forecasts, yet their basis is harder to establish than often thought. Groups can diverge in allele rates without diverging in genetic value. Top-down methods gauging descent spread and bottom-up methods matching scores both fail to surely split true genetic gaps from flaws like population structure, sampling bias, and cross ancestry portability. Bias in phenotype tests and study design variety confound shifts.
arxiv-2605-23364: Gosteva and three colleagues find a missed scaling regime in the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a model of wavy, chaotic fronts. Between large-scale Kardar-Parisi-Zhang scaling and small-scale varied behavior sits a middle regime with exponent one, born as viscosity passes through zero. The pattern belongs to the inviscid Burgers class, the zero-viscosity limit of the KPZ equation. Renormalization-group analysis and direct simulations both support the finding, filling a gap between two known scaling laws.
arxiv-2605-23464: Long and colleagues propose unextractable protocol models for decentralized training, where each participant handles only part of a large network and no one ever holds the full weights. Their framework injects time-varying, random, invertible transforms at participant boundaries, keeping the network function intact while making cross-time assemblies incoherent. On two models, 10000 transforms leave perplexity unchanged, and applying a transform every 30 seconds adds just 3 percent latency. Gradient attacks on stitched parts need at least 60 percent of from-scratch training tokens, so extraction stays impractical.
arxiv-2605-23664: Shah and colleagues give closed forms for sample size estimation when validating a binary prediction model on C-statistic precision. An earlier method recast Newcombe's formula for the C-statistic standard error and solved it in steps in R and Stata. The authors derive seven novel closed-form solutions with different algebra systems and AI models. The new forms show how tools yield distinct yet equivalent answers. Their solutions match step-by-step estimates on examples while running 148000 to 264000 times faster in median time, with small differences among them.
arxiv-2605-23964: Hendrickx, Pavirani, and Develder propose two-stage battery control that stacks income from grid balancing and frequency reserve in power systems. First, data-driven Monte Carlo optimization sets a time-varying bid sequence for Frequency Containment Reserve, replacing bids that waste battery flexibility. Then a deep reinforcement learning agent trades flexibility in real time while guarding the battery's charge level to meet reserve duties. Against uniform baselines, the approach raised profit by 7.56 percent in tests, showing that varying bids can match reserve duties to changing imbalance chances.
arxiv-2605-24164: Bideh and three co-authors describe the CUNY submission to the CLPsych 2026 shared task on tracking mental-health change through social-media timelines. To infer dominant self-states in posts, they ensemble three open-weight language models by majority vote. Moments of change are predicted by supervised classifiers built on those self-state predictions. Mood-pattern summaries augment example labels from upstream stages, beating zero-shot and plain in-context baselines. The submission placed first on one task, fourth on two more, and third on the last.
arxiv-2605-24364: Hanxuan Ye and Hongzhe Li unify the scattered theory of multicalibration boosting, a method that keeps forecasts fair across many slices and subgroups. They show that even sharp, flexible models can stay badly miscalibrated, and that forcing calibration trades against predictive risk, with early stopping controlling the trade. Their framework covers existing variants such as multiaccuracy, BatchGCP, and BatchMVP, and pins down where boosting converges. It also extends guarantees for how multicalibrated models transfer when the data shifts.
arxiv-2605-24664: Andrzej Zdziarski and others show that the Cyg X-1 black-hole spin depends strongly on the model chosen. XRISM Resolve data come with simultaneous NICER and NuSTAR coverage in the hard state. The simplest reflection fit puts spin near its maximum, while Comptonization-based models favor low spin. Joint fits stay consistent with any spin value. Low spin also fits gravitational-wave constraints. All models place the inner disk edge within ten gravitational radii, pointing to an outflowing disk corona also invoked for the polarized X-ray signal.
arxiv-2605-24964: Jiaxiang Li leads ConFi-GS, a fix for sharpening 3D scenes built from low-resolution views. Thin high-frequency evidence leaves 3D Gaussian splatting blurred, with weak edges and inconsistent views. Past fixes spread super-resolution guidance evenly or pick regions by geometry alone. They miss two distinct questions: where detail is needed, and whether candidate detail is reliable enough to internalize. ConFi-GS first maps detail demand from geometry, then weighs frequency reliability. One unified scheme injects only reliable detail, lifting fidelity and suppressing unstable detail.
arxiv-2605-25264: Victor Schvöllner links split graphs to number theory through the combinatorics of 2-switches. For a split graph, those switches are encoded by a factor graph whose induced cycles run at most four edges long. He asks for which numbers n some split graph's factor graph contains a triangle with every edge repeated n times. The answer turns on a purely arithmetic condition, the delta property, about differences and sums of complementary divisors. That condition joins graph theory to number theory in both directions.
arxiv-2605-25664: Majhi and Mondal present PostureClip, a collar-clipped device that blocks laptop work at a bent angle by darkening the screen until posture improves. Sensors and feedback give users live posture readings. In a four-week office trial, 165 people worked over six hours a day at a laptop. One group got no feedback, one got alerts plus screen darkening, and one got nothing. The feedback group improved posture angle and cut bent-angle time significantly against both other groups, and users praised its ease, timely feedback and habit-building effect.
arxiv-2605-25764: Zhao and colleagues present SpaPath-Bench, a benchmark diagnosing what tissue model codes encode about tissue space. Current benchmarks judge models by clinical endpoints, revealing little about whether embeddings distinguish tissue regions or capture spatial relationships. SpaPath-Bench turns spatial domain identification on paired slide and transcriptomics data into a diagnostic task. It curates 42 paired slides and tests 19 encoders with seven methods. Across 83,000 runs, it finds different pretraining approaches capture distinct aspects of tissue spatial architecture. It offers guidance for building spatially aware tissue models.
arxiv-2605-26064: Rouzbayani, Roy, Villagra and Jiang present Paris 2.0, the first video generation model pretrained by decentralised compute. It extends Paris 1.0, the first open-weight decentralised diffusion model, which showed image generation need not rely on one giant cluster. Coherent video had stayed open under decentralised training, and Paris 2.0 closes it. At low resolution, it cuts Fréchet Video Distance from 561.04 to 279.01 against a single-cluster rival on matched total compute, about a twofold gain. Text-video similarity and aesthetic scores also rise.
arxiv-2605-26364: Reza Namakian and five colleagues compute temperature-dependent stacking-fault free energies for random and locally ordered CoCrNi, using a near-quantum machine-learning model and an anharmonic tool. Simpler approximations suggested heat steadies the random state, but their results show its fault energy falls with temperature and stays below zero. Local chemical order, by contrast, keeps the energy above zero from zero to one thousand kelvin. Atom simulations confirm endless splitting in the random state but finite fault widths in the ordered state.
arxiv-2605-26464: Tingting Zheng and seven colleagues build a wide-field, high-detail mid-infrared upconversion imager that beats the crystal-aperture detail limit. An elliptical pump beam fits the narrow aperture of chirped-poling crystals, catching high sideways frequencies. Rotating that passband in Fourier space yields a run of images, which synthetic-aperture and phase-retrieval math fuse into one sharp picture. Resolution reaches 39 micrometers across a field 25 millimeters wide, a space-bandwidth product over ten times past records. The imager works at one photon per pulse per pixel.
arxiv-2605-26664: Aggarwal and Toninelli prove that single-flip Glauber dynamics for lozenge tilings of the size-N hexagon mix in time N to the power of 2 plus a vanishing term. The bound was predicted for general domains of diameter N by the Lifshitz law heuristic but previously shown only where the limit shape lacks frozen facets. A multi-scale comparison between the evolving height function and a volume-tilted limit shape unlocks the hexagon case.
arxiv-2605-26764: Ooyama and three colleagues simulate late gas infall onto protoplanetary disks older than 1 million years to test whether it can sustain stellar accretion. Much infalling gas is lost to photoevaporation, so steady accretion needs a way to strip angular momentum and pull gas inward. Strong viscosity does the job but spreads disks too wide, while magnetic disk winds remove momentum without expanding the disk. Infall torque alone can also drive inward flow and boost accretion.
arxiv-2605-26864: Chastenet and twenty-eight colleagues use JWST mid-infrared spectra to study dust in the inner circumgalactic medium of galaxy NGC 891. The mid-infrared glow out to 4 kiloparsecs comes mainly from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not hot dust, proving these large molecules survive in the inner halo. The 11.2 micron band dominates, pointing to more neutral, larger molecules, with little processing across height and radius.
arxiv-2605-27064: Nam proposes a valid machine-learned global proposal for Monte Carlo sampling in SU(2) lattice gauge theory. A coupling-flow update transforms active links conditionally on frozen links, staying invertible and preserving the product Haar measure, so it embeds into a Metropolis-Hastings correction without a full density. In two-dimensional SU(2) tests, the learned proposal matches the target ensemble. A mixed-step hybrid gives a modest sample size gain per runtime, but the work is a proof of principle, not proof of superiority over tuned schemes.
arxiv-2605-27264: Kawashimo and co-authors use a temperature-resolved Monte Carlo method to find where helium-burning rates most shape nickel-56 output in pair-instability supernovae. Thousands of stellar evolution runs show that the triple-alpha and carbon-alpha rates both peak in sensitivity near 250 million degrees, but with opposite correlation signs. That heat marks the regime where sampled rate shifts leave their clearest imprint on the pre-carbon-burning carbon-oxygen mix. The result means supernova nickel yields can probe helium-burning rates in specific low-heat regimes.
arxiv-2605-27764: Yuchen Guo, Junli Gong, Hongmin Cai, Yiu-ming Cheung, and Weifeng Su introduce SegWorld, a segmentation model that reasons before committing to a mask. Before any instruction arrives, it watches the scene first, noting visible objects and guessing events they may support. Given an intent-level instruction, it chains from the key object through the needed action to the physical touch site, lifting mask prediction on intent-level tasks.
arxiv-2605-27864: Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng, and Zihan Chen build a team of AI analysts for fundamental investment research, where the goal is a clear, checkable memo rather than a trading tip. In FundaPod, agents playing roles such as value investor or macro strategist work apart under shared rules for sourcing claims, then a human manager settles their disagreements. A full case study shows the design in action.
arxiv-2605-27964: Wang and colleagues model driving risk as a moving field rather than a single safety number. DRIFT spreads risk by a physics-style equation fed by speed-shaped kernels, hidden hazards behind large vehicles, and merge-zone pressure. On real traffic data it answered occlusions faster and cut near-collisions under occlusion against baselines.
arxiv-2605-28064: Lelia Erscoi and Tomi Kinnunen test how well people spot synthetic speech when asked to mark odd parts. Fully fake clips fooled hearers more often than chance, while trust cues moved conduct but not scores. Voice quality scores still rose and fell with clip type, showing a quiet sense of fakes where open spotting failed.
arxiv-2605-28164: Stegherr and colleagues ask what real users want from evolution-style optimizers on physics-based tasks. Across five expert cases, every expert wanted quick arrival at good answers plus some account of how answers formed, while other wants shifted by case. The paper lines up known methods with those wants and shows a rift between lab work and field use.
arxiv-2605-28264: Villani and colleagues fingerprint language-model hallucinations in the shape of token-entropy distributions, not just their average. Their Calibrated Entropy Score merges mean and peak entropy signals through a calibrated reference, needing one forward pass and black-box logits alone. Across eight question benchmarks and ten generators it led single-pass black-box detectors, nearly matching far costlier multi-sample methods.
arxiv-2605-28564: Barbara Maria Mayer and five colleagues dope hexagonal boron nitride with carbon using an electron beam in low-pressure methane. The beam creates vacancies and splits methane into single carbon and hydrogen atoms. Raising methane pressure curbs pore growth and drives triangular boron-ended pores through preferential hydrogen etching of nitrogen. Time-resolved spectroscopy shows carbon entering the lattice in hexagonal patches under one nanometer, with most carbon-rich regions confined to the irradiated area and some atoms drifting a few nanometers beyond it.
arxiv-2605-28664: Vijeta Deshpande and four colleagues test whether activation steering can supply training data for safety detection models. Safety detectors need examples of Helpful, Harmless, Honest-violating outputs, which are scarce, so the authors steer model responses toward target concepts. Across four concepts, two models, and four steering methods, stronger steering cuts response diversity, and steered data beats prompting data on three of four concepts. Yet only 41 of 136 steering setups beat prompting, so useful data sits in a narrow zone where success, coherence, and diversity all hold.
arxiv-2605-28764: Edwin Jose proposes SwarmHarness, a decentralised protocol where skill nodes form a compute swarm with no boss. Three parts interlock: a registry on a hash table for peer discovery and ads, and a router sending tasks by capability, load, latency, and trust. Credit rewards contributors via a Shapley-value guess. Nodes earn credits serving tasks and spend credits submitting them, while idle nodes drain credits and lose place. As nodes focus on high-reward skills, routing signals act as pheromones, and the network shows emergent group smarts like swarms.
arxiv-2605-28964: Victor dos Santos and colleagues identify prime numbers with a quantum protocol run on IBM processors. Primality is tied to Fourier components drawn from entanglement evolution in a two-part quantum system. Noise is tamed by a global rescaling factor, calibrated on a subset of circuits and extrapolated across setups. A new analytical bound for the Fourier modes, assuming a uniform starting superposition, widens the gap between primes and composites under moderate deviations, moving number theory closer to noisy-device practice.
arxiv-2605-29164: Kenneth B. A. Benício and colleagues propose a tensor-based sensing method for smart surface-aided communication systems. A higher-order singular value decomposition of the received echo jointly reads target delay, Doppler, and angle. Each parameter is read individually at low cost, with side-by-side computation as a bonus. Against a baseline that ignores the signal's tensor structure, tests show the same results at far lower complexity.
arxiv-2605-29264: Wei Lu and Qilong Zhai apply the weak Galerkin method to nonlinear eigenvalue problems of Gross-Pitaevskii type. They prove that the scheme gives a lower bound for the energy. Also, by a follow-up technique, they obtain a lower bound for the ground-state eigenvalue. Experiments validate the theory. The paper thus extends this toolkit to this class of problems with strict bounds on both the energy and the ground state.
arxiv-2605-29564: Victor Kowalski, Chengxi Li, and Dongheui Lee present VE2VF, distilling a vision-enabled teacher into a vision-free student for contact-rich manipulation. Vision helps manipulation but overfits to training visuals, so the student relies only on pose, twist, and wrench sensing. Training runs entirely in the real world without domain randomization or data augmentation. On an assembly benchmark board the approach reaches 95% success after about fifty minutes on three tasks. It generalizes to eight unseen variants, and fine-tuning with distillation reaches full success on the hardest task.
arxiv-2605-29864: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Andrew Melnik, and Michael Beetz ask whether short future videos can guide multi-step robot manipulation. They formalize Future-Experience Conditioning, which steers closed-loop policies with a latent future clip. Future clips use three stages: a reasoner over a task ontology, a digital-twin rollout of intended motion, and a diffusion model. The reasoner works from the scene. The diffusion model renders a robot-consistent clip with no segmentation at runtime. Generated futures beat no-future conditioning while mismatched futures hurt, and cloning plus reinforcement-learning leads.
arxiv-2605-30364: Chitraksh Singh, Monisha Dhanraj and Akram Sheriff propose the Hamiltonian Transformer, a physics-based way to spot radio senders that keeps signal size fixed in each head. It uses a skew-symmetric maker and a leapfrog step. Tests use raw radio signals from the WiSig set under four test types. The model hits about 99 percent right on same-day tests and about 62 percent with 150 senders, beating CNN and Transformer base models. A phase step at the input helps most.
arxiv-2605-30664: Tuero and colleagues improve policy tree search guided by a learned policy, which pays heavy overhead for explicit subgoal generation. They replace explicit subgoals with a learned rerooter inside the introduced square-root Levin tree search algorithm, which implicitly splits problems into soft subtasks. Three rerooters are proposed: one clustering by global state structure, one using learned cost-to-go estimates, and a hybrid of both. Avoiding explicit subgoal reconstruction enables scalable search with far lower overhead, reaching environments where subgoal-based search fails with strong online training efficiency.
arxiv-2605-31164: Yuanjian Xu and colleagues schedule language-model training data by modelling how samples influence one another. Most schedulers adjust the overall data mix while ignoring directional effects between samples, yet training order matters when samples push each other in specific directions. Their D3 framework builds a dynamic influence graph from loss-based dependencies and solves a constrained optimisation over it to order the data. The method improves on existing schedulers in both pretraining and post-training, with modest extra cost.
arxiv-2605-31464: Khan and colleagues study language models as selective stand-ins for GPU kernel runtime tuning. Tuning a kernel normally needs repeated on-device measurement, and each run is costly since it needs compiling and rerunning. A good stand-in should forecast relative speed well, and know when it might be wrong, deferring to the GPU then. The team finds models can forecast relative kernel speed accurately. Reinforcement learning sharpens both forecasts and confidence, and the stand-in lets a search test several times more candidates on the same GPU budget.

arxiv-2606-04164:
Sotirios Vavaroutas, Yu Yvonne Wu, Ali Etemad, and Cecilia Mascolo propose ADAPTOOD in 2026, a way to fine-tune heart-signal models when deployment data drift away from training data. Electrocardiogram models meet new sensors, new populations, and new tasks, and standard adaptation treats every shift as equally severe.

Their framework measures data uncertainty to grade how far the new data sit from the pretraining distribution, then lets that severity score steer low-rank updates and automatic tuning of training settings. The result adapts hard when the shift demands it and gently when it does not. In out-of-distribution tests, the method gained up to seven percent accuracy and nearly thirteen percent precision over existing approaches, and held up as shift severity grew.
arxiv-2606-04264:
Zeyuan Yang and a team of co-authors propose UniCanvas in 2026, a diffusion model that generates images with real text drawn inside them, rather than emitting text as separate tokens. Unified models usually must choose: autoregressive systems reason well but draw poorly, while diffusion models draw beautifully and garble words.

UniCanvas treats the image as a shared pixel canvas, a kind of world model of visual change, and learns language as visual patterns on that canvas. The model therefore paints words as naturally as it paints objects, interleaving them in one synthesis pass. Experiments showed it improving over previous unified models on mixed text-and-image generation. The authors position text-in-image diffusion as a promising route to a single model that both understands and creates across modalities.
arxiv-2606-04364:
Dhanesh Ramachandram proposes in 2026 a concept bottleneck model whose named concepts must look at the right body parts. Such models predict interpretable attributes before the final label. But a concept head for the wing is usually free to peek at the beak. It can then answer correctly for the wrong reason.

His part-factorized design ties each part query to one body region by construction. A learned spatial prior, seeded from average keypoint positions, guides the tie. A small alignment loss nudges each query toward its keypoint. Aligning on well under one percent of training images moved pointing accuracy from near chance to about three quarters of full supervision. Bird classification accuracy barely moved across the whole range.
arxiv-2606-04564:
Böhm, Purucker, Hutter, and Schlosser teach a tabular foundation model to predict when an event will happen, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard models predict what class an example belongs to. It must handle censored data, where follow-up ends before the event occurs. Standard foundation models cannot do this natively. Their predictions get biased. Their model, SurvPFN, is a prior-data fitted network. It is pretrained on millions of synthetic survival tasks. It can then answer new datasets without fitting each one.

The synthetic tasks use Weibull-distributed event times. Training uses a censored negative log-likelihood. So the model learns survival as continuous-time distributional regression. On SurvSet, a collection of real-world survival tasks, SurvPFN proved competitive with classical and deep survival baselines. It needed no per-dataset fitting. It needed no survival-specific architecture or feature engineering. The trick is treating censoring inside the loss itself.
arxiv-2606-04864:
Zhou, Fu, and Chung present a preconditioner that makes very large sparse linear systems solvable in practice, in a 2026 arXiv numerical mathematics paper. Symmetric positive definite systems from elliptic problems with varying coefficients are notoriously slow for iterative solvers, because low-energy modes converge slowly. Their two-grid algebraic multiscale preconditioner builds a coarse space directly from the system matrix, using graph partitioning and local generalized eigenvalue problems to create basis functions capturing exactly those troublesome modes.

The method needs no geometric information, so it suits unstructured, matrix-only settings, and its construction parallelizes naturally. On heterogeneous Darcy flow problems, numerical results show robustness to coefficient contrast and problem size, better performance than standard algebraic multigrid on challenging large-scale cases, and good parallel scalability.
arxiv-2606-05464:
Nicolas Astorga, Nabeel Seedat, and Mihaela van der Schaar introduce OPT-star in this 2026 arXiv paper, a family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating step-by-step reasoning in language models. Training with verifiable rewards has improved math and coding reasoning. But real decisions are wider: the challenge is finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid options.

Each OPT-star task ships with a feasibility checker and an evaluator. A complexity parameter expands the search space without new human labels. The authors study two training regimes. One uses a classical solver as a value oracle for partial states, shaping rewards by rank. The other uses search-based offline reinforcement learning when no solver exists. They link success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Training on OPT-star improved step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.
arxiv-2606-05664:
Gideon Lee links fault tolerance and gauge theory by a single construction in a 2026 arXiv paper. The spacetime code views a quantum circuit's whole history as one error-correcting code. Dynamical phase research, meanwhile, treats fault tolerance as a stable process over time. Lee gauges the spacetime code, a standard move that turns global rules into local ones. The result is a lattice gauge theory that inherits the circuit's fault tolerance.

In the new theory, Gauss laws encode when two error patterns count as equivalent. Wilson loops play the role of detectors, the checks that flag errors. Three applications follow. The theory covers layered computation, yielding a gauge view of measurement-based quantum computing. It also describes the classical memory of certain mixed topological states. Its detector observables match exactly what can be learned about circuit noise. One construction thus serves error correction, condensed matter, and learning theory.
arxiv-2606-05764:
Qiliang Lin, Qian, and Zhou prove lasting solutions for a magnetized fluid with partial damping in a 2026 arXiv paper. Magnetohydrodynamics couples a conducting fluid to a magnetic field, as in fusion devices and the Sun. Their three-dimensional system damps motion only horizontally and the field in one direction. A steady background field points sideways. Prior proofs needed every part of the starting state to be small.

The new result drops that demand for the vertical parts. Only the horizontal parts of velocity and field must start small. The vertical parts may be arbitrarily large, in a standard smoothness measure. New energy estimates, split by component, tame the dangerous cross terms. The background field's structure does quiet work throughout the proof. The theorem breaks the full-smallness barrier that limited earlier work. It widens the proven-safe starting states for anisotropic plasma models.
arxiv-2606-06064:
Mahajan and Chopra settle how many regions lollipops can carve from the plane, for most small counts in a 2026 arXiv paper. A lollipop is a circle with a ray stuck on it. Overlap many, and the plane fragments into regions. Paulsen's argument used two obstructions, one about stem directions, one about circles meeting at obtuse angles. The authors recast it as a weighted problem on two graphs.

One graph tracks stem pairs that stay apart; the other tracks circle pairs that fail to intrigue. Paulsen had bounded their overlap by one graph alone. Keeping the overlap term explicit and studying near-extremal configurations sharpens everything. All gaps close up to seventeen lollipops, and the nineteen case falls too. Eighteen and twenty lollipops narrow to a single missing region each. A recreational-looking problem turns out to hide extremal combinatorics. The two-graph bookkeeping is the paper's reusable tool.
arxiv-2606-06464:
Mandana Samiei and co-authors compare human and machine scientists in this 2026 arXiv paper on causal learning. Adults are famously bad at conjunctive rules, where an effect needs several causes present together, while handling either or rules well. Most evidence comes from passive tasks where learners just watch limited data. The team asked whether the handicap survives when people can run their own experiments, using a modified blicket detector task where objects may or may not activate a machine.

Letting adults intervene freely improved their conjunctive reasoning a lot, though such rules still took more tests than disjunctive ones. Language models in the same setup told a different story. Some top models neared human accuracy at naming the rule, but explored less efficiently and showed the same conjunctive gap. The authors conclude that choosing informative tests, not just receiving data, is where human causal learning shines.
arxiv-2606-06564:
Kehan Wang adds one well chosen summary to a transformer's memory of itself in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep transformers route information through residual streams. Block level routing methods compress each block's many updates into a single cumulative vector. That summary forgets the block's internal trajectory. HAARES keeps it and adds a second basis vector: the difference between the block's first half and second half updates, a coarse early versus late contrast, scaled to match and updated online.

Experiments on OpenWebText and character level benchmarks show a depth dependent pattern. Gains are small or mixed in shallow models but reliable at forty eight layers. In the two hundred one million parameter setting, HAARES beat the baseline on all three random seeds. A larger probe pointed the same way. Ablations rule out trivial explanations like extra sources or random details. The cost is modest extra memory.
arxiv-2606-06764:
This companion study asks the same generalization question for the most common network shape. Junyu Zhou, Wang, Lei, Ying, and Zhou focus on deep ReLU networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. ReLU is the standard activation that passes positive values and blocks negative ones. Earlier optimal results covered mainly shallow networks.

The authors give a full generalization analysis for gradient based training. Both plain and stochastic gradient descent are covered. They prove the first minimax optimal rates for deep ReLU networks. Minimax optimal means no method can promise better worst case rates. The conditions involve width growing with depth and sample size. Under those conditions, gradient methods match kernel methods on new data. The conclusion section restates the rate in formula form. It frames the work as closing a clear gap in deep learning theory.
arxiv-2606-06964:
Quivers are directed graphs whose representations form a rich algebraic world. Liu measures one family of those representations in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is the covering tree of the generalized Kronecker quiver. That quiver has two vertices joined by n arrows. Its module category splits into components, some of them regular.

For each regular Auslander-Reiten component, Liu defines two numbers. The width counts how broad the component runs. The second counts its flow modules, a special distinguished kind. He proves the width is at least half of that count, plus a half. A clean consequence follows at once. Every positive integer occurs as the width of some component. So the set of possible widths is exactly all natural numbers. The result gives a complete answer for this invariant, in a setting where classifying all modules is hopeless for three or more arrows.
arxiv-2606-07064:
Can boundary measurements reveal an unknown source hidden inside a curved region? Cârstea and Ghosh answer yes for a famous nonlinear equation in this 2026 arXiv paper. The equation is Monge-Ampère, where the determinant of second derivatives equals an unknown positive source. Solutions are convex functions pinned to prescribed boundary values. The slope at the edge is what an observer can measure.

The authors study the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, which sends boundary values to those edge slopes. Their theorem says this map determines the source uniquely. The proof cleverly uses very large boundary data. Big boundary values straighten the problem until it reduces to the X-ray transform. That classical tool recovers a function from its line integrals, and it is known to be injective. Inverse problems for fully nonlinear equations rarely yield such clean uniqueness.
arxiv-2606-07464:
Liang and a team compress a self-driving system's memory without discarding what decisions need, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-action driving models consume token sequences that balloon when they encode temporal context, breaching real-time budgets. Existing compression uses fixed heuristics like temporal decay, which can drop decision-critical moments. Their framework, COMPACT-VA, compresses context through a conditional vector-quantized autoencoder guided by planning intent: a latent summary of what the driver plans to do, distilled from trajectories.

A prior encoder predicts that intent from the compressed observations, and the policy plans using the bounded memory plus predicted intent. Evaluation focused on scenarios where history matters most, such as stopping, yielding, and proceeding at interactions. Under comparable token budgets, success rates improved by over 6 percent relative to heuristic compression, reaching about 68 percent. Closed-loop driving kept performance while running over 3 times faster and using under half the memory.
arxiv-2606-07564:
Young documents a design exercise for the next particle collider's detector, run as a long dialogue with an AI assistant, in this 2026 arXiv report. The Future Circular Collider's electron-positron mode would run a 15-year precision physics program in a 91 kilometer tunnel near Geneva. The AI proposed detector concepts from its assumptions; the physicist challenged subsystems in turn, from beam pipe to luminosity monitor, forcing revisions grounded in calibration, stability, and simplicity rather than headline performance.

The design evolved from the starting concepts through that exchange. Young is clear about the report's purpose: what a resulting concept could do remains unexplored, and the value lies in the process. The account is offered as a lesson on the promise and the limits of human-AI collaboration in experimental design. There, an assistant's first guesses need expert pushback to become engineering sense. It reads as a case study in machine creativity.
arxiv-2606-07864:
Dong and Song answer a question of S. T. Yau about when a curved three-dimensional space must really be flat, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is an asymptotically flat manifold, a space that looks Euclidean far away, with non-negative scalar curvature and curvature energy normalised to at most one. The positive mass theorem says such a space has non-negative mass, zero only for flat space. Yau asked whether small mass forces flatness in a strong, quantitative sense.

The answer is yes. Building on their previous work, the authors prove small mass yields a bilipschitz diffeomorphism to Euclidean three-space. That is an identification distorting distances by at most a fixed factor in both directions, far stronger than sharing a topology. The result quantifies the stability of the positive mass theorem's rigidity: near-zero mass cannot hide a very different geometry when curvature energy is controlled.
arxiv-2606-08164:
Jiangshuan Pang and co-authors ask a question every medical imaging lab pays for but rarely examines: how much preprocessing brain MRI scans need before pretraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Preprocessing pipelines define what a foundation model sees, yet are treated as routine cleaning rather than a modelling choice with a price.

Holding the corpus of twenty thousand brain MRI volumes, backbone, and protocol fixed, they compared eight graded preprocessing levels, P0 through P7, for two self-supervised methods. They then transferred the encoders to four downstream tasks. The lightest levels proved numerically unstable, making P2 the cheapest feasible choice. Beyond P2, picking the best level bought only about three point four points of aggregate utility for one method and one point eight for the other. Most gains were statistically unresolved. Stronger preprocessing helped mainly one task, and its edge could largely be recovered by preprocessing harder at transfer.
arxiv-2606-08464:
Lianyu Hu and colleagues let multimodal models look back at the image while they think, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chain-of-thought reasoning, where a model spells out intermediate steps, helps language models solve problems. But in multimodal models the reasoning happens entirely in text. After the image is first encoded, its visual features become inaccessible. The authors call this vision-blind reasoning, and it limits fine-grained visual extraction and error checking.

Their framework, TVI-CoT, interleaves textual reasoning with fresh visual feature access through learnable control tokens. Special tokens signal when the model should think in words, when it should look again at the image, and when it should answer. This switching lets the model re-examine the picture mid-argument, verifying a claim against the pixels rather than its memory of them.
arxiv-2606-08664:
Majumdar reports on particle detectors built in India for imaging with cosmic rays, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Muography is a passive imaging technique. It uses cosmic-ray muons to map the density inside large or hard-to-reach objects, from pyramids to cargo containers. Majumdar's group is developing a small prototype system that identifies materials by how muons scatter in matter. The tracking device is the Thick-GEM detector, a scaled-up, robust version of gas electron multiplier technology.

Several prototypes a few centimeters across were built by a local industry partner, with small changes in design from one to the next. After conditioning, each underwent detailed tests to check its fitness for the task. Domestic fabrication matters here: imported detectors are costly and supply-constrained. A robust local design could put muon imaging within reach of Indian laboratories and security uses.
arxiv-2606-08764:
Bob Osano tackles the backreaction problem in cosmology in this 2026 arXiv paper, asking whether the lumpiness of the real universe changes its expansion. Backreaction is the effect that clumped matter might have on the smooth expansion of the standard Friedmann model. Using a method that averages the universe over cells, he derives three results from the matter power spectrum, a curve showing how strongly matter clumps at each scale.

First, he proves a floor under the backreaction term: it cannot drop below the value simple linear theory gives, however clumpy matter becomes. Second, he shows the usual step-by-step approximation breaks down exactly where clumping turns strongly nonlinear. Third, he gives an exact formula for the information neighboring cells share, finding a value near one tenth for nearest neighbors at a scale of fifty megaparsecs. That shared information also measures the correction backreaction makes to the expansion energy budget.
arxiv-2606-08964:
An, Kim, and Ling ask how few coordinates it takes to embed an error-correcting code into a self-orthogonal one, over the integers modulo four, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-orthogonal codes, whose codewords are mutually orthogonal, are prized because they yield quantum codes. Embedding adds columns until self-orthogonality holds, and the shortest extension is the target quantity. The authors work with linear codes over Z4, the integers mod four, tied to nonlinear binary codes.

They prove tight bounds on the shortest embedding length, determined exactly under conditions including the quaternary Preparata codes. Along the way they classify the shortest doubly even self-orthogonal embedding length for binary codes in every case. When the two lengths coincide, their algorithm constructs all shortest embeddings. Running it produced 12 Z4 codes whose minimum Lee distances beat every comparable entry in Aydin's database.
arxiv-2606-09064:
Wang and colleagues teach video question-answering models to gather more visual evidence and double-check their answers against it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long videos hide evidence in a few segments, and most models use one search intent and one answer. Their framework, CoVER, expands the query into pseudo-queries and retrieves zoomed-in evidence widely. It drafts an answer and extracts a clue from the draft, then verifies the answer against the visual record with it.

The design shifts long-video understanding from answer-centric to evidence-centric reasoning. Results backed the approach. CoVER beat its baseline across benchmarks, with gains of 3.9 percent on MLVU and 4.6 percent on LVBench, plus smaller gains elsewhere. The 7-billion-parameter CoVER model outperformed same-scale models and surpassed closed-source systems on some metrics. Seeing more and thinking deeper complement each other: broader evidence helps only if conclusions are interrogated against it.
arxiv-2606-09264:
Sofia-Eirini Kotti and colleagues untangle overlapping brain signals in ultrasound movies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Functional ultrasound images brain activity indirectly, measuring blood volume changes that follow neural firing through neurovascular coupling. The task is blind separation, unmixing signals without knowing them, while undoing each source's hemodynamic response, the slow blood-flow echo blurring timing.

Their model treats multi-trial ultrasound data as a tensor decomposed into blocks. Each source is represented spatiotemporally: a low-rank spatial map plus a piecewise-constant firing signal convolved with that response, plausible in shape but varying by trial and source. A constrained optimization framework computes the split via projected gradient descent. In tests it recovered the maps and activation time courses across noise levels. Estimating that response proved the hardest part, marking where future work should aim. For a cheap modality, such unmixing turns blood-flow movies into neuroscience.
arxiv-2606-09364:
Martí Bosch checks whether cheap temperature sensors can be trusted for tracking city heat in this 2026 arXiv paper. Swiss cities such as Bern, Lausanne, Neuchâtel, and Zurich now run dense networks of low-cost devices that map heat street by street. Their weakness is radiative overheating: sunlight warms the sensor itself, inflating readings when shielding is poor.

Bosch builds a statistical correction based on incoming short-wave radiation, fitted with a generalised additive model, a flexible curve-fitting method. The correction was calibrated by placing each sensor model beside a professional MeteoSwiss weather station near Bern. He then asks how corrections change two heat indices, counts of tropical nights and official heat warnings. Official stations outside the cities underestimated heat warnings, while some cheap sensors overestimated them before correction. Even uncorrected, though, the city sensors described urban temperatures better than the rural reference stations did.
arxiv-2606-09464:
Parkosidis and his co-authors confront a long-standing puzzle in binary star evolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classical theory says tides should circularise a star's orbit before it starts transferring mass to its companion. Yet wide binaries that have already interacted commonly keep eccentric, oval orbits, and the eccentricity grows with orbital period.

Their general mass-transfer model, GeMT, is the first complete framework handling mass transfer in orbits of arbitrary eccentricity. They confront it with observations of hot subdwarf B stars, stripped stars whose formation histories are tightly constrained, paired with main-sequence companions. The model reproduced all observed orbital parameters without any fine-tuning, and oval orbits emerged from the transfer process itself. The final ovalness also depends on measurable quantities such as transferred mass and accretion efficiency.
arxiv-2606-09664:
Tuan Vu, Harri Lähdesmäki, and Julien Martinelli tune a tabular foundation model for a special search task in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization is a thrifty way to hunt for the best design with few tests. In latent space, the hunt runs over coded forms of things like molecules. Tabular foundation models now lead at regression and serve as stand-ins inside such hunts.

Their quirk is the training mix: these models learn their Bayesian habits from huge fake task sets. Latent-space hunts warp the map from code to score, so the habits fit poorly. The team adds fake hunt tasks, drawn from a molecule coder's latent space, to the pretraining stage. A regularizer anchors the model to its first form, so broad skill is kept. On held-out molecule hunts, the tuned model scored strongly.
arxiv-2606-09764:
Lawrence Jang, Mareks Woodside, and Geronimo Carom build a phone-agent test that is personal by design in this 2026 arXiv paper. A good phone agent should know its owner: their past orders, trips, contacts, and tastes, all stored on the device. Past tests use blank sandboxes with no such past. iOSWorld instead seeds one fixed persona across twenty-six fresh iOS apps.

The set holds one hundred thirty-three tasks in three grades. Single-app tasks test one app at a time. Multi-app tasks span two to eight apps. Memory tasks ask the agent to infer habits from the stored past. The best setup passed fifty-two percent overall, but just thirty-seven percent on multi-app work. Extra screen-tree access helped top models by up to twenty-six points, while small models gained nothing.
arxiv-2606-10064:
Bansal and colleagues argue that competitive agent arenas can manufacture the training data small models need, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Post-training agents requires multi-turn trajectories with per-trajectory judgments. Synthetic data from frontier models inherits their biases and loses the long tail, while raw production logs are unjudged and contaminated by shortcuts. Their testbed is a Bittensor subnet running ShoppingBench, an agentic commerce benchmark, as a scored competition.

The arena's race mechanism, language-model judge, and rotating problem suite produce incentive-aligned diversity with held-out evaluation guarded against memorization. Post-training Qwen3-4B on the filtered corpus lifted its success rate from eighteen percent to about forty-three percent on held-out tasks. That lands within noise of a synthetic-data baseline trained only with supervised fine-tuning, showing arena traces are a viable substrate.
arxiv-2606-10364:
Wang benchmarks the steps needed to turn Mars rover photos into printable 3D terrain models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Her pipeline finds stereo depth from NASA Curiosity images, completes the missing shape, and exports watertight meshes in OBJ format for printing. On the standard Middlebury stereo benchmark, a learned matcher clearly beats classical block matching on disparity error and coverage.

On Curiosity imagery, however, the learned matcher's denser depth maps show weaker edge alignment and higher reprojection error, hinting benchmark accuracy does not transfer to Martian terrain. Shape completion involves trade-offs. Alpha shapes preserve accurate but broken-up structure, and Poisson reconstruction yields coherent meshes but adds surfaces not in the data. A fixed diffusion-fill baseline sits between, sensitive to stereo quality. Standard methods can produce printable models, she concludes, but reliable rebuilding needs stronger domain checks.
arxiv-2606-10464:
Balaji and colleagues tackle a weakness of speech recognition in this 2026 arXiv paper: models trained on typical speech stumble on noisy rooms, phone-quality audio, dialects, or children's voices. Their fix, GC-LoRA, adapts a pretrained model cheaply with small trainable parts, following LoRA's low-rank update idea. It also inserts short-range convolutional processing, borrowed from Conformer models, so the adapter can hear local sound patterns that global attention misses.

Across test sets covering degraded, band-limited, dialectal, and child speech, GC-LoRA cuts the word error rate by up to 10.9 percent relative to compared baselines. It beats standard LoRA while using fewer trainable parameters. The authors read this as evidence that a small amount of local structure, placed inside the attention output, is an efficient route to acoustic adaptation.
arxiv-2606-10564:
Song, Lee, and Pickett analyse the electronic structure of a new nickelate in this 2026 arXiv paper in condensed matter theory. Nickelates are nickel oxide compounds, cousins of the cuprate superconductors. The material, La3Ni2O5F, has formally monovalent nickel and an almost perfectly two-dimensional character. Band calculations reveal an electron band from no atomic orbital: it is built from interstitial density, charge in the crystal's empty spaces, forming a cylindrical Fermi surface.

This band coexists with the conventional nickel-oxygen band, and the two behave oppositely, one electron-like and one hole-like. The authors call this a dichotomous electronic system. The band also partners with nickel d bands to form an incipient Dirac point. The authors predict the split should carry into the superconducting state.
arxiv-2606-10664:
Chiappori and colleagues test how much spouses can commit in this 2026 arXiv paper on household economics. In the collective model, partners bargain toward efficient outcomes, but the force of the bargain depends on commitment. Full commitment binds future behaviour; none renegotiates everything; limited commitment binds only until a partner prefers to walk away. The authors derive tests separating all three regimes from the dynamic effect of wage shocks on labour supply, using sign restrictions from theory to reject limited commitment too.

Applied to EU-SILC data from 15 European countries over 2005 to 2019, the tests find the bargaining weight rises after a favourable wage shock, the empowerment effect limited commitment predicts. Full and zero commitment are rejected in all but 4 countries; limited commitment survives everywhere. Household promises are real but conditional: a pay rise today shifts bargaining power, and who works how much, for years.
arxiv-2606-11264:
Zhaohui Wang, Huang, and Bian propose OmniBioTwin in a 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for health digital twins. A health digital twin is a dynamic, patient-specific model of health and disease. Current twins are fragmented: single-organ models lack cross-scale fidelity, while system-level twins lack a general architecture. OmniBioTwin treats twins as modular entities coupled through explicit interaction operators.

It, called a System-of-Twinned-Systems, organizes the twins in seven coordinated layers. They span data integration, autonomous twin modeling, cross-scale coupling, temporal synchronization, and human-in-the-loop decision support. The authors demonstrate it with a multiscale twin for GLP-1 signaling pathways in Alzheimer's disease. There, molecular, cellular, and organ-level twins are composed and coupled inside one system. They present the design as a scalable, readable foundation for precision medicine.
arxiv-2606-11364:
Ahmad studies anomaly-driven transport in pseudospin-1 Weyl semimetals in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Positive longitudinal magnetoconductance and planar Hall conductance are hallmark signs of the chiral anomaly in Weyl semimetals. Theory now extends Weyl fermions to multifold systems with higher-pseudospin quasiparticles. Ahmad asks how their anomaly-driven transport behaves.

He uses semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory with momentum-linked scattering and orbital moment terms. The planar Hall response needs broken azimuthal symmetry, supplied two ways: a tilt of the dispersion, and misaligned electric and magnetic fields. Untilted, the response is positive and quadratic in field strength. More scattering drives a sign reversal to negative values. Tilt changes the angular response into sine and cosine forms along each axis, giving strong anisotropy and a nonmonotonic tilt effect.
arxiv-2606-11764:
Huachao Zhang and Chang-An Zhao construct special error-correcting codes from algebraic curves in this 2026 arXiv paper. Linear complementary pairs and complementary dual codes matter for protecting hardware against side-channel and fault injection attacks. Recent constructions build them from function fields, but depend on non-special divisors, certain configurations on a curve with the right numerical properties.

The authors study Kummer extensions, a broad family of function fields defined by a simple power equation. They characterise non-special divisors whose support may include places that are not totally ramified, a widened class earlier work excluded. Using it, they explicitly build such divisors of the two key degrees on the famous GK curve and on general Kummer extensions, exploiting pure gaps. A general framework for complementary pairs of algebraic geometry codes follows, with security parameters determined inside it, plus a route to complementary dual codes.
arxiv-2606-11964:
Apashanka Das, Souvik Ghose and Tapas K Das study gas falling into a black hole in this 2026 arXiv paper. The flow is the Michel solution: spherical, steady accretion that passes from subsonic to supersonic speed. Real accreting gas mixes components, so the authors let the adiabatic index, which measures how pressure responds to compression, vary with radius.

They construct the stationary transonic solutions and draw phase portraits of Mach number against radius. A dynamical systems analysis sorts the transonic points; the relevant ones are saddle type, as expected for inviscid flow. Shaking the steady flow slightly shows it is stable. That analysis yields something striking: sound waves inside the flow obey an effective acoustic spacetime, with a horizon where the flow turns supersonic. Carter-Penrose diagrams display this emergent geometry's causal structure. Accretion thus doubles as a laboratory for analogue gravity.
arxiv-2606-12164:
Klein and co-authors build a statistical method that judges which influences on extreme pollution are straight and which are curved, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Regulators care about threshold breaches, which live in the upper quantiles, the high slices of a pollutant's distribution. Quantile regression models those slices, and additive forms let each factor bend freely. The catch is telling a factor's straight-line part from its curved part, which standard spline tools blur.

Their method, QDReSS, uses a Demmler-Reinsch basis splitting each effect into linear and nonlinear parts at right angles. Spike-and-slab priors, settings that can switch each part off, then select what matters via a Gibbs sampler. Simulations show both parts are estimated consistently and beat the standard mixed-model approach. Applied to Madrid air data, extreme nitrogen dioxide levels are driven differently by weather and by traffic-shaped spatial patterns.
arxiv-2606-12364:
Anamaria-Roberta Hartl and co-authors run a head-to-head race among the architectures challenging the Transformer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transformers pay quadratic attention cost as sequences grow. Subquadratic rivals, recurrent, state-space, and linear-attention designs, promise cheaper scaling. Three leaders, xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet, anchor hybrid models. Standard language benchmarks barely separate them, so the authors test on complex domains: code and time series, where long-range structured dependencies expose architectural biases.

Each backbone is trained from scratch and also distilled from a Transformer teacher. Broad reasoning and commonsense tests prove insensitive to backbone choice. Code generation separates them much more sharply. Mixing experiments vary how many subquadratic layers replace attention layers. One xLSTM-heavy mix leads on a mixed corpus at twenty billion tokens, while a leaner ratio leads on pure code. The paper distills principles for choosing operators by domain.
arxiv-2606-12464:
Bhoi and co-authors test a modified-gravity cosmos with a neutral measuring tape, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The VCDM model tweaks gravity minimally so the vacuum energy can drift with time, adding no new particles. A reported transition feature in its expansion history had raised interest. But features can be artifacts of how data are fitted. The authors instead use cosmography: describing expansion through its kinematic series, fitted with a Padé approximation that stays well-behaved.
