The package runs in Python and ships with tutorials and a friendly website. It is free on public code and package sites. Better alignment should sharpen downstream study of how cells are regulated across data types.
pmc-13199564:
Amany Tarek and colleagues derive exact wave solutions for light pulses in magnetic-optic channels in a 2026 theory study. Solitons are self-holding light pulses prized for fast data links. Standard models gloss over how magnetism and strong nonlinear effects interact, so the team solved a fuller paired equation system.

Using an improved equation method, they found a fresh set of exact solutions. Shapes include kink and anti-kink fronts, which flip between two levels, plus sharp singular profiles. Tuning key nonlinear settings gave precise control over pulse stability and front steepness. The math may guide high-capacity optical links and all-optical switches, devices that route light with light.
pmc-13202164:
Living with several chronic diseases at once complicates self-care, and a 2026 protocol headed by Ana Lúcia Junger sets out a systematic review on how patients' beliefs shape their behavior. The protocol examines illness perception and self-management in adults with multimorbidity, an area where evidence from single diseases may not transfer.

Grounded in the Common-Sense Model of self-regulation, the review will search seven databases for observational studies using validated perception measures. Two reviewers will select studies, extract data, and judge quality with established scales, and a meta-analysis will be run where the data allow. The goal is to link beliefs about causes, control, and consequences to adherence and self-care.
pmc-13209764:
A tracking tag that folds like paper and shrugs off acid is presented in a 2026 engineering study led by Meng Zeng. The research article designs a miniature radio-frequency identification antenna from graphene film on a flexible plastic sheet, folding one arm behind the tag instead of adding connectors through the material.

The finished tag measures only twenty-four by thirteen millimeters yet tunes into the standard UHF identification band. Adjusting the folded arm shifts its resonance, and a stepped arm plus matching network achieved near-perfect power transfer to the chip in testing. Performance held after corrosive soaks and a thousand bends, with a read range beyond a meter.
pmc-13212164:
Megan K. Wasson and co-authors surveyed fertility specialists in 2026 about a common judgment call: whether to remove uterine fibroids that do not distort the womb cavity before infertility treatment. Such fibroids may still harm the uterine lining, yet practice varies widely.

The survey reached medical directors at 407 United States clinics, and 112 physicians replied. Most respondents said they weigh removal, often once a fibroid reaches roughly four to six centimetres or more. About 42 percent operate themselves, while the rest refer patients to other surgeons. The authors call for clearer evidence on which fibroid types truly warrant surgery.
pmc-13212264:
Sovannmony Lay and a multinational team report in 2026 on the nutritional value of ten farmed freshwater fish species sold in Cambodia. Fish supply most animal protein in the country, so knowing what farmed fish actually contain matters as wild inland catches decline.

Laboratory tests measured moisture, protein, fat, minerals, and fatty acid patterns for each species. Protein and fat levels varied widely, and saturated fats formed the largest share in most fish. One species, walking catfish, delivered strikingly high amounts of two healthy omega-3 fats in a small serving. The data give public health planners a firmer base for dietary advice and farm policy.
pmc-13212864:
Zongsheng Yuan and co-authors report in 2026 a soil treatment built from leftover enoki mushroom material turned into biochar and loaded with helpful bacteria. Their target was poor coastal sandy soil, tested with a hardy shoreline plant.

After thirty days, the combined treatment raised soil nitrogen and potassium sharply and more than tripled two enzyme activities linked to nutrient cycling. Beneficial bacteria became more dominant, and the microbial community reorganised. Plants responded with roots roughly twice as long and far more numerous, plus stronger defences against stress damage. Turning farm waste into a living soil amendment could help restore difficult coastal land.
pmc-13215164:
Pierre-Luc Thériault and colleagues show in 2026 that a thin organic film can double the frequency of light inside a chip guide. The film is laid down as vapour and needs no electric poling step. Such doubling feeds new light sources, fast switches, and tools that make paired photons for quantum work.

The film bends light by very unlike amounts for two wave types. That gap let the team sync a wave with its doubled twin while the two still overlap well. Their guides hit a yield on par with the best lithium niobate chips. Since the film coats almost any base, plain chips could gain these light tricks. The result puts self-aligned organic films on the photonics map.
pmc-13215664:
Sheila O'Brien and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for developing a group therapy aimed at combat veterans with moral injury. Moral injury follows acts or betrayals that violate a person's sense of right and wrong, and no first-line treatment targets it directly.

The project uses user-centred design in three steps. Interviews with veterans and Veterans Affairs clinicians and chaplains will surface needs and barriers. A treatment manual will then be drafted and revised with an expert panel, and two small open trials with twelve veterans will test the draft in practice. Recruitment for the pilot trials ran from October 2023 to January 2025. A randomized trial would follow if the manual proves usable and acceptable.
pmc-13216164:
Nayne Vieira da Silva and co-authors present a 2026 veterinary case report of a cancer never before documented in cattle. The tumour is a carcinoma of the rete testis, the network of tubules at the centre of the testicle. The patient was an eight-year-old Nellore bull referred for blood in its semen.

Ultrasound showed dilation of the central testicular tissue with fluid-filled cystic spaces. After surgical removal, microscopy revealed an infiltrative tumour confined to that central region, and staining tests showed the cells carried both vimentin and cytokeratin but not a blood vessel marker. On that combined evidence the team made the diagnosis. They advise adding this rare tumour to the list of possibilities when bulls show blood-stained semen or cystic changes.
pmc-13216264:
Tsumugi Shoji and co-authors present a 2026 cell biology study of how the immune sensor STING is switched off. After STING sounds the alarm over stray DNA, lysosomes swallow and destroy it; the hand-off step was not understood.

Working in cultured cells, the team shows that two lysosome components are indispensable for that swallowing step: a membrane fat called PI(3,5)P2 and CHMP4B, part of the ESCRT-III machinery. Binding tests place CHMP4B directly on that fat. A mutant CHMP4B that cannot bind it failed to restore STING destruction in cells missing the normal protein, and signalling stayed on. The authors present this pairing as the mechanism that ends the innate immune signal at the lysosome surface.
pmc-13216764:
Nihangma Patangwa and co-authors present a 2026 dental case series on fixing a gummy smile the gentle way. Two patients showed excessive gum display with small, spaced upper front teeth, traced to altered eruption patterns that leave crowns looking short.

Treatment combined surgical crown lengthening, by gum removal and bone reshaping, with a three-month wait for the gumline to settle. The teeth were then built up directly with a bioactive nano-hybrid composite rather than ground down for porcelain. Standardized pink and white aesthetic scores improved, tooth structure was preserved, and gum health held. At about two years, the team noted only minor chipping and mild plaque-related inflammation, with gum levels broadly stable, while flagging the lack of longer-term data.
pmc-13217164:
Keerthi Miryala and co-authors present a 2026 computational chemistry study of two closely related light-absorbing dyes built around a barbituric acid acceptor. The question is why near-identical structures behave so differently when excited by light.

Density functional calculations showed the first dye staying rigid and planar on excitation, its electron cloud barely reorganizing, a locally excited character with weak response to solvent. The second dye flexed along its donor-to-acceptor axis, shifting charge strongly toward the acceptor, polarizing further in polar solvents, and shrinking its energy gap. Photovoltaic descriptors followed the same split: the second dye aligned well for injecting electrons into titanium dioxide with strong light harvesting, while the first looked unsuitable. The authors frame rigidity versus charge transfer as the design lever.
pmc-13218164:
Huazheng Cao and colleagues track how the back surface of the cornea shifts over five years after a laser procedure, in a 2026 retrospective study. Keratorefractive lenticule extraction reshapes the cornea by removing a lens of tissue. A bulge of the posterior cornea can signal instability and raise ectasia risk, a thinning disorder. Which tissue thicknesses predict that shift matters for screening before surgery.

The study followed 165 patients, measuring posterior central elevation at twenty-seven points across central and peripheral zones. Measurements ran from three months to five years. The cornea shifted forward, then returned to baseline by five years. The center moved backward while the periphery moved forward. A thinner cornea mattered most: patients below 500 micrometers faced roughly three to six times the raised-elevation risk. Residual bed and lenticule thickness correlated with the shift, while cap thickness did not, so the authors urge caution with thin corneas.
pmc-13218464:
Xinjuan Zhou, Xinrui Li, Haiyi Chen, and Jing Deng evaluate China's employee medical insurance outpatient pooling reform in a 2026 study. The reform pooled costs into shared funds, widening coverage for clinic visits once paid for alone. Using 2018 data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, the team asked whether the scheme changed outpatient use among people aged forty-five to sixty.

Three models examined visit chances, visit counts, and out-of-pocket spending. Residents of pooling regions had a five-percentage-point higher chance of an outpatient visit and higher visit frequency. Expected out-of-pocket spending was still about forty-eight percent higher in policy regions, a tension the authors report without resolving. Places offering richer outpatient benefits showed stronger responses, and people with several chronic conditions used more care. The authors read this as improved access to unmet needs, while flagging design questions.
pmc-13218564:
Katie M. Babbott and a large team report user experiences with a well-being app for young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 qualitative study. Young people with the condition face psychological distress, yet scalable support services are scarce. The Lift app, built for emotional well-being, had completed a twelve-week feasibility trial in New Zealand and the United States.

Thirteen from that trial, nine users and four support people such as parents and partners, joined focus groups or interviews about the app. Analysis followed a rating framework covering engagement, how well the app worked, its look, and its quality. Participants found Lift engaging, easy to use, and affecting, praising features like a well-being tree that grew with use and the calming design. Several described emotional or behavioral shifts, including connection, self-awareness, and better coping with diabetes. The feedback will guide refinement of the app.
pmc-13218764:
Aidan Shulkin and co-authors review facial reconstruction performed with the patient awake in a 2026 paper combining a literature review with cost analysis and practical guidance. General anesthesia has been the default for facial rebuilding, but it brings perioperative risks and resource use. Operating under local or regional anesthesia avoids those costs, yet the approach remains underreported and its best practices unsettled.

Thirty studies covering 1,249 patients and 1,262 flaps met the review's criteria, with forehead and nasolabial flaps the most common. Minor complications affected about ten percent of flaps and major ones under three percent, most patients reported little or no pain, satisfaction ran high, and nobody needed conversion to general anesthesia. A forehead flap done awake cost about 1,280 dollars against roughly 6,647 dollars under general anesthesia, a saving above five thousand dollars per case. The authors supply a guide to patient comfort and argue the technique deserves a wider role.
pmc-13220464:
Yufang Niu and colleagues show that a noncoding RNA in chickens encodes a small protein that steers growth in a 2026 study. Long noncoding RNAs were defined by not making proteins, yet ribosome profiling catches some of them in the act of translation. The team compared RNA production and ribosome activity between precursor cells that were multiplying and those that were maturing.

Of 178 noncoding RNAs that changed between states, three were differentially translated, and one, named lncMPD, carried coding potential and ran high in multiplying cells. It produces a seventy-four-amino-acid peptide, MPD-74aa, which the team confirmed by antibody detection and mass spectrometry. Adding the peptide pushed cells to keep dividing and held back maturation into muscle. The peptide binds CDK1, a cell-cycle protein, and raises its abundance. The authors present the finding as a new regulatory layer in muscle development, with relevance to poultry breeding.
pmc-13221064:
Donrawee Waeyeng and co-authors investigate plant foods and kidney health in a 2026 cross-sectional study from southern Thailand. Ninety-six residents aged fifty or older lived with environmental exposure to cadmium and lead, metals that can damage kidneys. The question was whether eating more plant foods still helped under that exposure.

Blood metal levels, diet scores, and several kidney markers were measured during routine screening in late 2024. People eating more plant foods showed lower levels of a urine marker for tubule cell injury. Nuts and seeds stood out most clearly. The authors also flag that urine marker as a possible early warning test for metal-related kidney damage.
pmc-13222364:
Eman S. Sabry and co-authors present a sensor-based smart driving test system meant to replace human judgment with measured results, in a 2026 engineering paper. Sensors and a control chip log how a test taker actually drives, producing steady scores. A working model demonstrates the concept, built for uniform, scalable license exams.

The paper weighs technology readiness, cost, rollout, and legal compliance, with a detailed cost model. Set against platforms abroad, the design's data links, modular hardware, and screens stand out. Planned upgrades include machine learning to predict outcomes, low-power radio links, and cloud dashboards. The authors frame automated testing as a route to fairer testing and stronger public trust.
pmc-13223964:
Kiana Kawarizadeh and co-authors describe a 2026 immunology study centred on VPS33B, a protein that helps compartments inside cells fuse. Earlier work linked faulty VPS33B to a rare syndrome affecting joints, kidneys, and bile flow. The new work asks what the protein does in dendritic cells, which show fragments of microbes to other immune cells.

Removing VPS33B from dendritic cells weakened their display of peptides on MHC class II molecules, and CD4 T cell responses fell as a result. Responses that depend on CD4 help also suffered, while direct CD8 priming stayed intact. The cells mainly displayed leftover pieces of the invariant chain, pointing to a loading fault.
pmc-13230664:
Biachew Asmare and colleagues assess in 2026 drinking water quality in Debre Markos town in northwestern Ethiopia. Sixty-six samples came from boreholes, disinfection points, household taps, and storage containers in a 2024 study. Lab tests covered chemical traits such as acidity and nitrate, plus germ counts that signal fecal contamination.

Most chemical measures met World Health Organization guidance, aside from warm source water. Protective chlorine left in water fell below advised levels at sources, taps, and homes, though levels were fine right after disinfection. No harmful germ markers appeared at disinfection points, yet most tap and home samples carried coliform bacteria. Guarding sources, keeping disinfection steady, and treating water regularly are urged to close the gap.
pmc-13230864:
Omar Alkhazragi presents in 2026 an optical computing system that keeps memory and processing together using a laser array. Normal chips lose time and energy moving data between memory and processor, a snag known as the Von Neumann bottleneck. Tiny surface-emitting lasers can switch very fast and sip power, which suits small devices.

The array performs the repeated pattern-matching steps that image networks need, reaching hundreds of millions of convolutions each second in the demonstration. Reported accuracy was near ninety-eight percent for the computing tasks shown. Fast low-power optical math could help driverless cars and drones run vision models on board. Scaling the laser approach may prove easier than growing chip-based optical systems.
pmc-13232164:
Samantha Velazquez and colleagues use in 2026 magnetic floating to reveal that identical nanoparticles wear surprisingly different protein coats. Blood proteins coat any particle entering the body and decide how cells treat it. Standard tests blend millions of particles, which hides differences between single coats.

Their sensitive setup floats particles at heights set by tiny density gaps, sorting one batch into distinct layers. Protein checks across layers found more than five hundred proteins shifting in an orderly gradient. Top layers leaned toward blood and outside-cell proteins, while lower layers gained structural and energy proteins. Coat variety built into every batch could explain why some nanomedicines behave unevenly in the body.
pmc-13232864:
Habib ur Rehman and colleagues develop in 2026 a four-step iteration for finding points that two special mappings share unchanged. Fixed point results guarantee solutions to equations without always giving a way to compute them. The mappings here stretch distances in a controlled one-sided way, and pairs of them arise in shared-solution problems.

The new scheme builds a sequence from both mappings at once and is shown to settle toward a common fixed point. Weak and strong convergence results cover different space conditions, backed by worked examples. The method is then applied to nonlinear integral equations of a specific class in Banach spaces, with an example validating the approach. Iterative schemes like this turn existence claims into numbers engineers can use.
pmc-13233064:
Evangelia Baka and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study on how human factors shape artificial intelligence in health care across low- and middle-income countries. Most guidance on AI ethics comes from wealthy settings, leaving local realities understudied. The team interviewed 21 AI researchers and innovators working across Latin America, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East with North Africa.

Five themes ran through the interviews. Oversight needs people who are ready and trained to provide it. Ethics training is scarce, and systems built elsewhere often fit local conditions poorly. Governance should center human needs, and multidisciplinary teams help bridge the gaps. The authors call for investment in AI education and inclusive governance so these tools narrow health gaps instead of widening them.
pmc-13233564:
Wugui Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 study testing a cancer drug, KPT-330, against osteoarthritis in mice. The drug blocks exportin-1, a protein that ferries molecules out of the cell nucleus. In osteoarthritis, bone-eating osteoclast cells under the cartilage help drive joint damage. The team used mice with surgically triggered joint disease and cultured osteoclasts in dishes.

Treated mice kept more of their under-cartilage bone, preserved cartilage, and formed fewer osteoclasts. In dishes, low doses blocked osteoclast formation and bone resorption without poisoning cells. The drug quieted two signaling routes, NF-kB and MAPK, and lowered the master osteoclast genes they control. The authors propose exportin-1 blockade as a two-way strategy against bone and cartilage damage.
pmc-13233664:
Jayco Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 rapid review of how to teach palliative care to oncology residents. Adding palliative skills to cancer care improves how doctors talk with patients, control symptoms, and make decisions, yet resident training varies widely. Searching literature from 2000 to 2025, the team found twenty studies of training programs for residents in cancer care.

Half the programs were immersive rotations inside specialist palliative services, usually lasting four to eight weeks. These rotations steadily improved how trainees talk with patients, control symptoms, and feel about the work, with no clear gain from going longer. Required rotations beat optional ones, producing broader gains and more change in real clinical behavior. Short courses and workshops formed the other half. The review feeds into work on shared training standards across Europe.
pmc-13234064:
Elisabeth Stöttinger, Beate Priewasser, and Eva Rafetseder published a 2026 developmental psychology study on why children cling to first impressions. When a picture slowly morphs from a rabbit into a duck, children keep calling it a rabbit long after adults switch. Three experiments with children aged three to eleven probed the reasons, replicating the earlier finding.

Away from the morphing sequence, children named the same images as readily as adults, so perception itself was not the problem. Only children aged nine and older matched adult timing in the gradual condition, and a focus on the whole picture rather than details helped. Telling younger children both possible answers in advance improved their switching, though not fully. pmc-13234364:

pmc-13236164:

pmc-13236564:

pmc-13236664:

pmc-13236964:

pmc-13238664:
Tanaka and colleagues close a patient's chest with plastic cables after emergency heart surgery, because metal was not an option. pmc-13239064:

pmc-13239764:

pmc-13239864:
Samuel Deakin and a large Canadian team map the genetic structure of woodland caribou across western Canada in a 2026 study. Ice age advances and retreats, plus modern habitat damage, have layered the animals' ancestry at several scales, and conservation units need to reflect that history.

The authors urge planners to protect diversity at every level of the hierarchy.
pmc-13240064:
Minoo Moghimani and co-authors gather published case reports of foodborne Campylobacter infection in a 2026 systematic review. pmc-13240264:

pmc-13240764:

pmc-13240864:

pmc-13240964:

pmc-13241464:

pmc-13241564:

pmc-13241664:

pmc-13242464:

pmc-13242664:

pmc-13243264:

pmc-13243764:

pmc-13245564:

pmc-13246064:

pmc-13247564:

pmc-13247764:

pmc-13248764:

pmc-13248964:

pmc-13250464:

pmc-13250864:

pmc-13253064:

pmc-13253264:

pmc-13253564:

pmc-13254264:

pmc-13254564:

pmc-13254764:

pmc-13254864:

pmc-13255164:
