pmc-13255664:
Remigiusz Gałęcki and co-authors report a 2026 rat feeding trial testing unusually high levels of yellow mealworm meal in the diet. Insect protein is attracting interest as a sustainable feed ingredient, yet safety at high inclusion rates needs checking. Rats received diets containing twenty-five to forty-five percent mealworm meal.

The animals kept stable growth, adjusting how much they ate so nutrient intake stayed even, and none refused the food. Heart and breathing rates stayed within normal ranges for their age. Some blood and chemistry measures differed between diet groups, though behavior tests showed no drop in activity, no anxiety signs, and no loss of curiosity. The authors conclude that high mealworm inclusion supported normal development under the trial conditions, backing its promise as a feed ingredient.
pmc-13255764:
Zejun Mo and a large team report a 2026 study of drought response in Blumea balsamifera, a medicinal plant whose active compound is L-borneol. Dry conditions limit both its growth and its chemistry, yet its internal drought machinery was poorly mapped. The team combined plant physiology with gene and protein profiling.

Drought suppressed photosynthesis and changed L-borneol accumulation in the plant. Roots switched on antioxidant and water-balance systems, protecting cells from stress damage. Photosynthesis-related genes and proteins were dialed down, with changes concentrated in the phenylpropanoid pathway, a hub for defensive compounds. The authors say the combined profile clarifies how this species tolerates drought and offers candidate genes for breeding hardier planting stock for medicinal production.
pmc-13255864:
Shinya Kajiura and Ryuji Hayashi present a 2026 nationwide benchmark of RET fusion findings in Japanese cancer genomic testing. RET fusions are rare but valuable, because selective RET-blocking drugs can help the patients who carry them. The first reimbursed profiling result often decides access to such treatment, so knowing normal rates matters.

Drawing on 97,343 cases in the national C-CAT system, the authors found RET changes in well under one percent of cases overall. Rates ran highest in chest tumors and in head, neck, and thyroid tumors. The five routine testing platforms reported somewhat different frequencies, while tissue and liquid biopsy pooled rates looked numerically similar. The authors stress the numbers describe practice patterns, not platform quality, and offer them as a reference for interpreting results.
pmc-13256164:
Natalie Fischhaber and co-authors report a 2026 methods study on growing the common-cold coronavirus HCoV-OC43 in realistic airway cell cultures. Cells grown at an air-liquid interface mature into layered airway lining with mucus, closely mimicking the human bronchial surface. The team used a structured experimental design to test seven variables at once.

Cell maturity emerged as the strongest factor: fully differentiated cultures produced significantly less viral RNA than immature ones, especially when virus was applied to the air-facing side. Infection from the tissue side behaved less consistently and depended more on dose size. Washing away mucus repeatedly before infection boosted viral growth in mature cultures. The authors hand future coronavirus researchers a recipe for robust infection in the most lifelike version of this model.
pmc-13258064:
Inga Jagemann and co-authors wrote a 2026 eye-tracking study of how app store ratings shape acceptance of an AI skin cancer screening app. Seventy-six participants viewed a mock app store listing under either positive or negative rating conditions while their eye movements were recorded. Forty-two saw the positive version and thirty-four the negative one. The team also surveyed perceived usefulness, ease of use, trust, intention to use, and willingness to pay.

Viewers spent the most visual attention on the app description, then the reviews, then the ratings, with price and data protection getting least. A single negative rating did not significantly change gaze patterns, usefulness, ease of use, trust, intention, or willingness to pay. Instead, intention to use was predicted by perceived ease of use, usefulness, and trust in the app itself.
pmc-13258164: Damian Dyńka and co-authors issue a 2026 fix to their 2025 study that weighed ketogenic diets against other diets for weight loss. The notice is a correction only. The funding note and the conflict note held errors, and both are printed in full anew. Funds came from a trust set up by two co-authors, who also helped draft the work. New entries name trust roles and side ventures for some authors. The authors state that their findings stand as before, and the first article has been updated.
pmc-13258864:
Péter Szatmári and colleagues ask whether obesity quietly rewires the transport proteins that guard male fertility. ABC transporters pump substances in and out of cells in the testis and sperm. Feeding rats a fatty, sugary diet for ten weeks, their 2026 study watches two of them closely.

The diet made rats heavier, glucose-intolerant, and left them with smaller reproductive organs. In the testis, one transporter's gene and protein output rose while a second transporter's message fell. In sperm, both transporters' messages dropped. Testosterone and its control genes stayed unchanged, suggesting fertility risks can start before hormone trouble shows.
pmc-13259664:
Cintia Birkenstok and coauthors study how a hormone related peptide drives drug resistance signals in colon cancer in a 2026 paper. Cell and animal models of colorectal cancer received the peptide alongside a standard platinum drug. A central growth pathway protein, beta catenin, was tracked into the cell nucleus.

The peptide pushed that protein into the nucleus in a modified active form. Treated cancer cells tolerated the platinum drug better in dish tests. Blocking the pathway supported its role in the resistance effect. Animal results split by model, with one mouse model showing reduced drug benefit and another showing none. Oncologists gain a caution on peptide rich tumor environments.
pmc-13261464:
Shu Tang and colleagues tested in 2026 a mixed fluid that coaxes more oil from layered reservoirs where water races through easy paths. In such fields, injected water channels through permeable streaks and leaves oil behind. Their system suspends thick oil droplets in water as the continuous phase, then drives it through sand packs and a transparent plate model.

The droplets jammed narrow spots in the fast layer through the Jamin effect, the resistance a trapped droplet creates. Permeability of that layer collapsed by more than tenfold, sending later fluid into the tight layer instead. Recovery from the tight zone rose by eight and a half percentage points, and the effect held through a faster push phase. Visual runs showed the channel-block-redirect sequence directly. The authors propose the method for mature, high-water fields.
pmc-13262364:
Guofu Mao and Haizhen Lan write a 2026 letter to the editor about drugs used to start anesthesia during emergency breathing-tube placement. They respond to a review comparing etomidate and ketamine in critically ill adults. That review found similar death rates, but more blood pressure collapse with ketamine.

Mao and Lan argue this short-term blood pressure gain should not make etomidate the default choice for all patients. They note that death estimates could still hide real gains or harms, and that one large study from Brazil linked etomidate to higher later death rates. Etomidate can also suppress adrenal glands, glands that help the body handle stress. They urge choices matched to each patient's state.
pmc-13262564:
Shoira Agzamova and Faniya Babadjanova follow the gut fallout of heart surgery in toddlers. Bypass machines save children with congenital heart defects but stress the whole body, gut included. Their 2026 prospective study samples twenty children before and just after cardiopulmonary bypass.

Friendly bacteria like Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus thinned out sharply after surgery. The short-chain fatty acids those microbes make, butyrate and propionate, fell with them. Longer time on bypass meant deeper disruption. Children with the worst gut changes struggled most with feeding, nutrient absorption, and weight gain. Watching the microbiome, they argue, belongs in postoperative care.
pmc-13262864:
Lara S Stahl and colleagues run a pilot trial of motherhood decision support for women with multiple sclerosis in a 2026 journal article. Multiple sclerosis is a long-term immune disease of the brain and spinal cord, often diagnosed during childbearing years. Many women feel unsure about pregnancy. The trial compared a web decision aid alone with the aid plus coaching by trained nurses.

The Germany-wide trial recruited 35 women over five months, 22 in the aid group and 13 in the coached group. Conflict about the decision fell in both groups by follow-up, more sharply with coaching. On a scale to 100, coached scores dropped from a median 49 to 15, versus 54 to 31 with the aid alone. Interviewees called both helpful.
pmc-13263364:
Yonghun Kim and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on stent repair of torn chest aortas after blunt trauma. The repair, called TEVAR, threads a fabric-covered stent through blood vessels to seal the tear. Success needs a healthy landing zone above the tear, and zones of fifteen millimeters or less are considered short.

The team reviewed 52 patients treated from 2018 to 2023, most with severe injuries. Twenty-nine had short landing zones, and five needed the left arm artery covered. Leaks around the stent occurred in three patients, one of whom died. Outcomes did not differ significantly between short and longer zones, supporting TEVAR even when the landing zone is short.
pmc-13263764:
Md Abdullah Kafi and colleagues trace a surprise alliance behind an erection drug's brain effects. Vardenafil raises levels of a signal chemical tied to memory, but its route in the brain was murky. Their 2026 study works in nerve-cell systems with chemistry, imaging, and live recordings.

The drug lifted amyloid-beta levels, which pulled the prion protein inward from the cell surface. That inward trip proved key: block the making of amyloid and the synaptic effect was gone. Exciting signals grew stronger on the sending side only, with more messenger release sites firing more often. Amyloid and prion protein, famous for harm, here serve plain synaptic tuning.
pmc-13264364:
Yu-Fang Huang and colleagues show that blocking complement brings back muscle cell function harmed by myasthenia gravis antibodies in a 2026 study. In this autoimmune disease, antibodies attack the receptors that receive nerve signals at muscle. Live-cell calcium imaging was used in human muscle cells. The team watched how patient sera and purified antibodies against receptor subunits upset signal-driven calcium waves. They also tested whether a complement C3 blocker could prevent that breakdown in the dish.

Antibodies against one subunit wiped out the calcium response, while those against another did not. Gene activity and membrane attack deposits were also counted. Complement blocking protected signaling in their system. Human cell evidence of this kind complements animal work and supports complement as a treatment target in antibody-positive illness.
pmc-13264764:
Guoqiao Li and colleagues evaluate microwave ablation for tiny low-risk thyroid cancers in a 2026 retrospective study. One hundred seven patients chose the needle heat treatment over surgery or watchful surveillance. Follow-up tracked lesion size, shrinkage rate, thyroid function and complications, then compared complete versus incomplete disappearance groups to find factors predicting success. Tiny papillary cancers grow slowly, so the balance between intervention burden and peace of mind drives much of this debate in thyroid care.

All treatments were completed successfully. Ablation zones briefly enlarged at one month, then shrank steadily, with maximum diameter clearly smaller by a year. Only a minority of closely followed lesions had vanished completely at that point. Hormone function measures were followed for safety. Longer observation will decide durability.
pmc-13264864:
Sindhu Bhaarrati Naidu and colleagues describe a United Kingdom cohort protocol for lung cancer in people who never smoked in a 2026 paper. Such cancers would rank among the top causes of cancer death if counted separately, yet their drivers and diagnostic delays are poorly understood nationally. The OLIVE study will build a multicenter group from health records, defining never-smokers by lifetime cigarette use below a set threshold, and extract occupation, ethnicity, exposures and outcomes.

Deep learning text analysis will mine free-text notes for details structured fields miss. Follow-up runs to death, withdrawal or five years. Planned outcomes span social and exposure predictors plus survival. Better recognition of this distinct disease could shorten diagnostic pathways for patients whose risk is often dismissed.
pmc-13265164:
Yue Hou, Yu Gao, and Wen-Ming Yan chart global research on radiotherapy for cervical cancer from 2015 to 2024, in a 2026 bibliometric study. Radiotherapy is a core treatment for this cancer. Mapping who publishes what can reveal hotspots and gaps. The analysis drew on a major citation database.

In all, 1,496 publications met the inclusion rules. Output grew unevenly, with a slight recent decline. China, the United States, and Japan contributed most. Leading topics included new radiotherapy technology, resistance mechanisms, combined immune therapy, quality of life, and unequal access. The authors point to precision treatment and personalised plans as future priorities.
pmc-13265264:
Chenghang Tian and the team test genetic links between frailty and preeclampsia in both directions, in a 2026 Mendelian randomization study. Frailty reflects reduced reserve with ageing, while preeclampsia is a dangerous pregnancy condition. Whether each raises the risk of the other was unclear. Genetic data from large public sources were used.

Genetically predicted frailty raised the odds of preeclampsia in two separate datasets. The reverse direction also appeared in one dataset, with preeclampsia raising later frailty. Multiple sensitivity checks supported the forward findings. The authors read their findings as suggestive of a two-way link that needs medical attention.
pmc-13266564:
Sidar Burcu Ateş Demiroğlu leads a 2026 trial comparing two laser treatments for carpal tunnel syndrome. In this wrist problem, a nerve is squeezed, causing pain and numbness in the hand. The trial enrolled 63 patients with 114 affected hands, all with mild or moderate disease confirmed by nerve tests.

Patients wore wrist splints and were split into low-level laser, high-intensity laser, and control groups. All groups improved over three months in symptoms, nerve tests, and scans. Both laser groups did better than the control group. No clear gap appeared between the two laser types, so the authors say either can boost standard splint care.
pmc-13266664:
Jie Zhang, Baiwei Zhang, and Chunjing He wrote a 2026 animal study on shock wave therapy for diabetes-damaged blood vessels. The therapy sends sound pulses into tissue and is used for some muscle and bone problems. The team tested it on the leg blood flow of rats with diabetic vessel disease.

Forty rats were split into five groups, including drug-treated and combined groups. Treated rats showed lower levels of a growth signal protein and its pathway. They also showed more of a vessel-wall marker in leg muscle, wider thigh arteries, and faster blood flow. The combined group showed the strongest changes. The authors link the benefit to calmer vessel growth signaling.
pmc-13267564:
Keyi Zhou and colleagues design in 2026 a detachable microneedle patch that treats white patches inside the mouth that can turn cancerous. The patch delivers copper-bismuth framework particles directly into the lesion, avoiding whole-body exposure. Inside abnormal mouth cells, the particles lowered a metabolic enzyme called PDK3 and triggered two forms of cell death at once: copper-driven cuproptosis and runaway self-digestion by autophagy.

That double attack suppressed the abnormal cells more strongly than either route alone would suggest. In animal studies, the patches cleared the lesions with little sign of harm to the rest of the body. The authors present the patch as a gentle, local option for a precancerous condition that today lacks good minimally invasive treatments.
pmc-13268464:
Viviane Mauro Corrêa Meyer and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter reporting a pilot study of a triple-drug therapy in cystic fibrosis. The drug combo, called ETI, fixes the faulty protein behind the disease and has transformed outlooks. Whether it also calms body-wide inflammation is less clear. The team followed patients from pediatric and adult clinics who started ETI during the study period.

Eight patients, with a median age of about twenty, were enrolled. Blood was drawn at the last visit before starting ETI and again months later. The team measured a panel of inflammation signals, including several interleukins and markers tied to neutrophils, the white cells that flood CF airways. They also compared lung function before and after. The letter presents this pilot design and its measures; the authors expected inflammation markers to fall on treatment.
pmc-13268764:
Amy Witkoski Stimpfel and co-authors dig in 2026 into why frontline registered nurses actually leave their jobs, using a national 2022 survey of nearly nine thousand nurses. Pandemic-era losses reshaped the workforce, and shortages are projected for years. Their analysis used regression to separate real turnover drivers from background traits.

Almost three in ten nurses had turned over. Dissatisfaction with the main job more than doubled the odds of leaving, and burnout, holding a second job, being in school, or holding a graduate degree also raised turnover. Union participation, by contrast, was linked to staying. The authors point to flexible scheduling as a quick lever for hospitals to improve satisfaction and keep experienced nurses.
pmc-13269164:
Kanami Ota and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about an 83-year-old woman with a rare intestinal lymphoma, a cancer of immune cells in the gut. She had lost 20 kilograms over a year and felt deeply tired. Scans showed thickened walls in two parts of her bowel that seemed to join.

A camera exam found an ulcer ring in her colon and a second opening beside it, leading toward the small bowel. Tissue samples confirmed the lymphoma, staged as Lugano Stage II. Surgery and drug treatment were judged impossible given the tumor site and her weak state. She received supportive care and died on hospital day 33. The authors say such an abnormal joining should raise suspicion of lymphoma.
pmc-13269264:
Yumi Abe and co-authors chart in 2026 the normal background uptake of a radioactive amino acid tracer used to image brain tumors, so that real tumors stand out more clearly. Fluciclovine PET scans were re-analyzed from twenty patients with suspected malignant glioma. Uptake values were measured in twenty-four defined head regions, and dynamic curves followed the tracer over time in most patients.

Normal brain uptake was low overall, lowest in white matter and slightly higher in deep structures such as the cerebellar vermis and pons. The pituitary and saliva glands peaked early then washed out, unlike the flat brain pattern. A comparison tracer, methionine, ran higher in every brain region, while fluciclovine ran higher in veins, muscle, and the nasal cavity. The baseline map aids reading of tumor scans.
pmc-13269564: A correction notice from 2026, for a 2016 paper led by Jun-hua Zhao, fixes one image in the extra files of a study on a long noncoding RNA in stomach cancer. In a cell cycle chart, the image for the SGC-7901 cell group had been copied by mistake from the control group image. The correct image has now been put in its place, and the notice links to the updated extra file.
pmc-13269964:
Mohammad Noor Katranjy and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 17-month-old toddler with a relapsing fever lasting 30 days. The fever responded only partly to fever drugs, and came with gut symptoms and a skin rash. No earlier COVID-19 infection had been documented for the child.

After wide clinical and lab investigations, doctors diagnosed multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, a serious complication that can follow COVID-19 in those under 19. The syndrome can look like several other diseases, which makes atypical cases hard to spot. The child was successfully treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, pooled human antibodies, and corticosteroids, drugs that calm inflammation. The authors present the case to aid early recognition.
pmc-13270264:
Ya-Fei Tian and co-authors map in 2026 a circuit by which busy neurons feed the growth of high-grade gliomas, among the deadliest brain tumors. Firing neurons and their support cells trigger an enzyme that clips a protein called neuroligin-3 from cell surfaces. The freed fragment reprograms tumor cells into a state eager to form synapses, through several internal signaling routes.

Reprogrammed tumor cells build working synapses that receive excitatory input from neurons, and calcium waves then ripple across the tumor network. Those waves stir the surrounding brain toward seizures, which drive still more activity, closing a growth loop. The authors organize counterattacks by circuit stage: calm the activity, block the clipping, jam the downstream signals or synapses, and retune the wider network.
pmc-13270864:
Salomé Porten is lead author of a 2026 secondary analysis, a new look at a past trial, asking whether poor sleep at the start predicts how well post-traumatic stress treatment works. Sleep problems are very common in PTSD and were feared to block the memory learning that trauma therapy needs.

The team studied 178 women treated for up to 15 months with one of two trauma-focused therapies. Sleep was tracked with a wrist device, diaries, and a standard questionnaire. None of these measures predicted symptom gains, depression did not change the picture, and results did not differ between the two therapies. The authors say sleep treatment need not come before trauma therapy here.
pmc-13271264: A short correction notice in mAbs for 2026 replaces the caption of Figure 2 in a study of antibody bivalency by Heirene and colleagues. The notice is a correction only, changing no data or findings. The new caption explains how antibodies that bind with one arm can pack more densely on a cell surface. It contrasts that pattern with two-arm binding, which presents fewer Fc domains to immune effector cells.
pmc-13271464: No author is named in the record for this 2026 notice of republication. It corrects an article on the molecular genetics of 103 sporadic colorectal tumours in Czech patients. The article was republished on February 12, 2026, with an updated supplementary table, S1 Table. The notice lists exact sentences to be added or amended in the methods and results. Those edits make patient features point to that table. They also make per-tumour findings on mutations, methylation, and staining point to it. The notice repeats several of the corrections verbatim.
pmc-13272164:
Yaning Yuan and coauthors review in 2026 the two-way relationship between sepsis and the gut microbial community. Sepsis, the body's extreme response to infection, both damages gut microbes and is worsened by that damage. The review separates human evidence, animal evidence, and unproven claims so readers can judge each safely.

Sepsis drives microbe imbalance through poor blood flow, inflammation, and heavy antibiotic use. The disturbed gut then feeds organ damage across brain, lung, liver, and kidney pathways. The authors warn that live probiotics are dangerous in septic shock and some other high-risk states, urging source control and careful antibiotic use first.
pmc-13272364:
Zhenyuan Xu and coauthors propose in 2026 that mitochondria moving between cells act as a shared economy inside tumors, redistributing energy capacity where stress demands. Cancer cells import healthy mitochondria from support and immune cells, restoring their power generation and drug resistance. Export also happens, and its direction is selective.

Damaged mitochondria dumped into killer T cells can corrupt their function, while healthy ones delivered to suppressive immune cells keep those cells active against the patient. Transfer routes include tiny tunneling tubes, vesicles, and cell fusion. The authors argue outcomes depend on donor, cargo quality, and recipient, opening treatment ideas around blocking the traffic.
pmc-13272464:
Huihan Wang and coauthors review in 2026 progress on the structural proteins of HIV-1 and the drugs that target them. The virus's Gag, Pol, and Env proteins run its life cycle, from assembly to entry into new cells. Blocking their functions remains a main engine of anti-AIDS drug development.

The narrative review covers recent inhibitor advances against each protein family and the mechanisms those drugs exploit. Resistance and delivery problems that limit current therapy receive attention as well. The authors close with design strategies for the next generation of antivirals, aiming at durable control of a virus that still infects millions worldwide.
pmc-13272564:
David M. Mannion and co-authors reported a difficult fungal infection after lung transplantation in a 2026 case report. A 60 year old man worsened six weeks after receiving two new lungs. Testing found a yeast called Trichosporon inkin in both his chest fluid and his blood.

Doctors confirmed the infection with biochemical tests and fungal DNA sequencing. Treatment combined drainage of the infected chest fluid, guided by imaging, with the antifungal drug voriconazole. Blood levels of the drug were checked and adjusted to reach a safe target. The authors say this is the first reported case with both sites infected at once. They stress molecular testing and firm source control in transplant care.
pmc-13272664:
Alkomiet Hasan leads a 2026 randomised trial testing whether an old blood pressure drug, spironolactone, can help thinking in schizophrenia. Brain signaling through a pathway called NRG1-ERBB4 is linked to memory problems in this illness. Animal work suggested spironolactone can adjust that pathway, prompting a proof-of-concept trial.

Ninety patients were assigned to 100 milligrams, 200 milligrams, or a placebo for three weeks, with working memory as the main outcome. Memory scores improved most in the high-dose group, but the planned analysis did not show a clear win over placebo. Later checks hinted at a benefit, and both doses were well tolerated, supporting longer or higher-dose trials.
pmc-13273064:
Jan-Etienne Pudell leads a 2026 study of ultrafast lattice motion in layered stacks of platinum and copper metals. Driving vibrations at terahertz frequencies in metals is hard, because free electrons spread energy quickly. The team made superlattices, repeating bilayers a few atoms thick, by sputtering, and probed them with femtosecond X-ray pulses.

They show electron pressure, not phonon stress, drives a large coherent vibration at 1 terahertz in these stacks. Modeling supported that reading. The effect can be tuned by layer pitch and materials. So the authors present electron pressure as a designable driver for ultrafast strain devices, including possible spintronic uses.
pmc-13273764:
Kim and colleagues compare two ways to predict leftover cancer after a breast biopsy that removes a lump. Their 2026 journal article studies breast MRI scans and biopsy margin results. Margin status tells whether cancer cells reach the cut edge.

The study included 170 patients who had an excisional biopsy. Residual cancer remained in 51.8 percent of the patients after surgery. MRI alone and margin status alone each missed some cases. Using both tests together raised sensitivity to 88.6 percent across the group studied. Together they also raised specificity to 80.5 percent for clearing cancer-free patients. Sensitivity means the share of cancers the tests catch. Specificity means the share of healthy cases they clear. The authors advise combining both before planning more surgery.
pmc-13273864:
Ahmad Aulia Jusuf, Fadilah, and Nimas Ayu Nirwanti tested lycopene against harm from reused cooking oil in a 2026 rat study. Heating oil again and again creates oxidants that can cross the placenta and damage developing organs, a real concern where oil reuse is common. Lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, is a strong antioxidant.

Twenty-four mother rats were split into six groups, receiving plain feed, heated oil at two doses, or oil plus lycopene through pregnancy and early nursing. The higher oil dose sharply reduced healthy neurons in two brain regions of the pups and raised liver cell damage. Lycopene recovered much of that loss across brain and liver measures. A cell death marker also rose with oil and fell with lycopene, which supports a protective effect.
pmc-13273964:
Hao Liu and co-authors measured wrist artery tears after heart catheter procedures in a 2026 retrospective study. Doctors increasingly reach the heart through the radial artery at the wrist, and the vessel wall can split during the work. How often this happens and how it heals were unclear.

Using a fine imaging method inside the artery, they reviewed 1,995 patients treated between 2016 and 2024. Tears appeared in about one patient in eight, usually shallow and limited. Older age, female sex, longer procedures, artery spasm, and narrower arteries all tracked with tearing. In a small group imaged again later, tears checked after a month had healed completely, mostly through smooth inner growth. The authors classify tear types by shape and depth to guide future care.
pmc-13274964:
Sonja Harkener and colleagues present a 2026 journal article assembling an up-to-date checklist for judging health research data quality. A data set is only useful if it is fit for its purpose, and quality can only be shaped during collection. The team merged three sources: a revised 2014 German guideline, a review of literature since 2013, and manual additions.

The resulting IDEFIM set holds sixty-nine indicators across fourteen dimensions of data and metadata quality. Consistency carried the most measures at nineteen, then accuracy and completeness at twelve each. The best-supported indicators were missing values, contradictions, and how current the data are. Metadata quality was covered far less often, and three indicators were newly added for diversity, equity, and inclusion.
pmc-13275064:
Judith Bossen and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on why the gas-exchange cells of fruit fly airways skip the local immune response. In Drosophila, tracheal terminal cells deliver oxygen to tissues, like tiny lung units, and constantly remodel their branching with food and oxygen levels. Bacterial infection triggers a strong defense in the rest of the airway lining.

These terminal cells, the team found, simply lack the bacterial sensor PGRP-LC, so the defense pathway never fires inside them. Forcing the sensor on caused branching loss, damage, and cell death, which blocking downstream factors prevented. Both remodeling and immunity need the same switch, FoxO, so staying immune-privileged protects the cells' life-sustaining flexibility, an evolutionary trade-off.
pmc-13276764:
Ayşenur Coşkun Toker and co-authors present a 2026 pilot trial of a brief psychological program for earthquake survivors in Türkiye. The 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes left millions with trauma amid scarce services. Problem Management Plus is a short, lay-deliverable program built for exactly such strained settings.

Seventy-six survivors in temporary housing were assigned by chance to the program or to enhanced usual care. Retention reached about three quarters and adherence about four fifths, supporting feasibility. Right after treatment, the program group improved more on every measure: depression, anxiety, distress, trauma symptoms, daily functioning, and self-named problems. The gaps were large, including a depression score difference of about six points. At one month, distress and personal problem gains held firm. The authors call for a full-scale trial.
pmc-13276864:
Jean-Baptiste Pérot and co-authors reply to a critic of brain imaging terminology in a 2026 letter. The exchange concerns scans called neuromelanin-sensitive MRI, used to study the substantia nigra in Parkinson disease. A commentator argued that T1 shortening is required before neuromelanin can explain the bright signal.

The authors accept that their sequence carries a magnetisation transfer effect, even without a dedicated preparation pulse. Slice comparisons show that this effect boosts contrast in the target region. Animal experiments at very high field show signal growing as neuromelanin accumulates over time. They conclude that both effects shape the image, and they defend the scan's value for tracking nigral degeneration.
pmc-13277664:
Eric J Stern leads a 2026 field report on a case of Legionnaires disease, a serious pneumonia, tied to a home device that mixes powdered infant formula. The patient was a ten-month-old girl with a condition that weakens the immune system. She was admitted in November 2025 with fever, fast breathing, and chest signs after weeks at home.

Blood and urine tests identified Legionella pneumophila, a bacterium that grows in warm, stagnant water. The same bacterium was found in household water and at higher levels inside the formula device. For immune-weakened infants, ready-to-feed formula may be safer, the report says. If powder is used, water should be heated well, then cooled, before mixing.
pmc-13277764:
Kazusa Nofuji leads a 2026 study of comprehensive genomic profiling, broad gene testing of tumors, for gynecologic cancers at one institution in Japan. Matching treatment to tumor genes is promising but still early in these cancers. The team followed 44 cases tested between March 2020 and July 2022 and tracked who received matched therapy.

Actionable gene changes, meaning changes with a possible drug match, appeared in nearly all cases. About a third of patients were judged candidates for matched therapy, yet only three actually received it. Worsening health and complications blocked others. One gene, PIK3CA, was tied to worse survival. Testing earlier in the illness, before health declines, could widen access to matched drugs, the authors say.
pmc-13279264:
Xue Hao and colleagues report a 2026 study of how aged cells drive swelling in old tissue. Aged, or senescent, cells build up with age and leak a mix of signals called SASP that fuel chronic swelling. The team study R-loops, three strand knots of DNA and RNA, and ask how they reach that leak.

They found R-loops pile up outside the nucleus, the cell control centre, in aged cells. From there they trip an innate alarm path called cGAS STING, which drives the leak of signals. A carrier pair, XPO1 and DDX1, ships the loops out of the nucleus. Blocking XPO1 with a drug cut the leak, eased age linked swelling and stretched health span in their model. The ship step gives a fresh drug target.
pmc-13279664:
Kimberly Cortes Perez and colleagues report a 2026 study that builds a free three dimensional library of kidney stones. Three dimensional stone models aid surgery training, teaching and computer vision work. No standard, open set split by stone chemistry existed. The team built a photo based pipeline: many photos from a spin stage and two fixed cameras turn in a full model.

Stones of five chemical types were shot, led by calcium oxalate stones. Most types rendered well, with five of five uric acid stones and three of three brushite type stones done. All cystine stones failed to render, a clear limit of the method. Twenty five kidney stone surgeons graded shape and surface truth on a five point scale. High grades backed the pipeline as a base for an open repository that labs can share.
pmc-13279764:
Zhenyu Lu and colleagues published a 2026 review of how metals and metalloids influence the PD-1 and PD-L1 immune checkpoint. It is the molecular brake tumors exploit to hide from the immune system, and that modern immunotherapy releases. Searching three databases through March 2026, the team gathered human, animal, and experimental studies on whether exposures to elements such as zinc and copper change checkpoint behavior.

Effects proved context-dependent, strongest for the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair and thin for other checkpoints. The mechanisms they catalog run through oxidative stress, low-oxygen signaling, inflammation pathways, and remodeling of the tumor's immune neighborhood. Those changes affect T-cell exhaustion and how well checkpoint drugs work. Blood measures tied to zinc and copper status emerged as candidate biomarkers. The authors caution that most evidence is preclinical, with little direct human data. They frame this research as a priority for further studies.
pmc-13280464:
Christopher Collin Hayes and team report a 2026 case of right sided heart failure in a child with Lutembacher syndrome. The syndrome pairs mitral stenosis, a narrowed heart valve, with an atrial septal defect, a hole in the heart wall. Signs vary with valve severity and hole size. Their patient was a thirteen year old girl with congenital stenosis and a secundum defect. She was lost to follow up for ten years.

Worse stenosis and a larger hole drove major left to right shunting of blood. Severe right heart overload, pulmonary hypertension and severe tricuspid regurgitation, a leaky valve, followed. Cath tests showed low cardiac output and high lung pressures. Surgery held mechanical mitral valve replacement, hole closure and tricuspid annuloplasty, a valve repair. Left heart weakness after surgery eased with drugs. At two years, both sides of her heart worked well and failure signs had fully cleared.
pmc-13280664:
Ziwei Wang and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on protecting the brain after a bleed inside it. A bleed harms brain cells at once and then keeps harming them for days. The review links three topics that are often treated apart. They are cell death, the birth of new brain cells, and stem cell therapy, meaning care that uses young cells that can grow.

The authors explain how blood, iron, and swelling set off more cell death after the bleed. New cells do form, but few live or link up well. Stem cells may help by sending signals that calm harm and aid repair. The review lists blocks to human use, such as poor cell survival and safety risks.
pmc-13281064:
Stefan Reuter and colleagues published a 2026 survey of how German transplant centers handle kidney transplants across blood group barriers when recipient antibody levels start high. Such ABO-incompatible transplants widen the living donor pool, but starting titers at or above 1:512 strain antibody removal, and practice varies. Twenty-seven of thirty-six invited centers answered a nineteen-question survey in early 2025 on testing, cutoffs, desensitization, and responses when antibody levels refuse to fall.

Nearly half the centers accept candidates at any titer, while the rest impose caps between 1:512 and 1:2048. Every center uses rituximab, and most remove antibodies with antigen-specific adsorption columns, sometimes backed by plasma exchange. Experienced centers were likelier to have dropped fixed cutoffs entirely. When a first attempt stalls, two thirds would retry after three to six months with intensified treatment. The authors call for harmonized antibody assays, futility criteria, and a multicenter registry to discipline the patchwork.
pmc-13281164:
Md Borhan Uddin and colleagues applied queue math to a heart ward in a 2026 study from Bangladesh. The Sylhet hospital serves a poor region where heart care is often delayed. The team used records for more than six thousand patients treated in 2023. They tracked arrivals, stays, and beds in four units, from standard care to the heart lab and two intensive units. Queue models show where flow jams when demand nears capacity.

Two intensive units jammed worst, with bed shortages that hurt care quality. The heart lab, by contrast, had beds to spare. The authors advise moving spare beds and growing the small intensive unit from eight beds to fifteen. The larger intensive unit would grow from ten beds to twenty-five. They also warn against piling extra beds into standard wards, which crowds care and hides the true shortage.
pmc-13281364:
Patrick Krastman and colleagues published a 2026 register study measuring what share of Dutch general practice consultations concern musculoskeletal disorders, aches and injuries of muscles, bones, and joints. Using a national database holding records for over 2.5 million patients from 2017 to 2023, they classified consultations by chapter and broke the musculoskeletal share down by age, sex, and body region.

Musculoskeletal problems accounted for 11.3 to 12.6 percent of all consultations across the period, making them the leading reason for visiting a Dutch general practitioner. Lower limb complaints led the regions, followed by back and upper limb problems. Women generated about 60 percent of these consultations, and the heaviest concentration sat in the 55 to 64 and over-75 age bands. With population aging advancing, the authors expect the share to grow. They frame the numbers as planning evidence for workforce capacity and for care models that keep musculoskeletal work from crowding out everything else in general practice.
pmc-13281464:
Ameer Hohlfeld and colleagues surveyed trial leaders in sub-Saharan Africa on publishing results in a 2026 study. Trials that never reach print can skew what doctors think works. The team emailed more than six thousand leaders found in a global trial registry. Four hundred nine took part in the web survey. They were asked about duty to publish, delays, and blocks they had met.

Most agreed trial leaders must publish all results, and most within two years. Bias in what gets printed was rated high for the region. Close to two thirds had printed at least one trial within two years. Yet about one in four had a finished trial they could not print. Top blocks were journal rejection, lack of time, and dull results. Three in four had no training in writing trial papers. The authors urge training and support for African teams.
pmc-13281764:
Emanuela Foglia and colleagues assessed full automation in an Italian germ lab in a 2026 study. Germ labs face rising sample counts with flat staffing. Machines that run the whole chain, from check-in to plate reading, promise relief. The team took a broad health technology view at one hospital lab. They compared hand work and machine work on urine samples and on blood cultures that had turned positive. Costs, staff time, and staff views were all weighed.

Automation cut check-in time by about two thirds. Seeding plates by hand all but vanished, and plate reading time fell steeply. Yearly staff costs for the tracked work fell by about two thirds too. Total handling time dropped by a like share. Staff reported safer work and a lighter load. The authors say the case rests on more than speed: freed hands can shift to harder tasks.
pmc-13281864:
Jun Zou and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a woman with a deadly fungal infection. She was thirty-nine and had just learned she carried both HIV and hepatitis C. The fungus spreads through the body in people with weak immunity and kills up to three in ten treated patients. Blood tests and cultures confirmed it had spread widely. She began a strong fungal drug at once. Her liver and kidneys then failed, and confusion set in as the liver faltered.

She was moved to intensive care in grave shape. Teams added a machine that does the liver's cleaning work from outside. A second machine took over the kidneys' filtering. The authors present the paired support as a rescue that pulled her through. They note that organ failure often caps drug doses in such cases. Their report adds rare guidance for this exact crisis.
pmc-13282164:
Taifu Huang and co-authors published a 2026 study modelling how climate change is shrinking habitat for the dhole in China. The dhole is a wild dog and top predator, listed as endangered worldwide and given the highest protection class in China. The team combined sighting records with climate projections in an ensemble model, a blend of several models, to map suitable habitat in past, current, and future periods.

Suitable habitat now covers about one million four hundred thousand square kilometres, mainly around the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. That area has fallen by nearly half since the past period studied. Future climate scenarios project a further fall of roughly twelve to thirteen percent. Cold-month temperature, height above sea level, and slope shaped past habitat most. The authors name mountain ranges, including the Qilian and Hengduan ranges, as future refuges, and call for larger protected areas.
pmc-13282264:
Mojtaba Aghaei and co-authors wrote a 2026 narrative review on two small genetic variants in a gene linked to leukaemia. Leukaemia is a group of blood cancers shaped by both genes and environment. The gene, BMI1, helps blood stem cells renew themselves and is tied to cancer growth. The review examines two single-letter DNA changes, named rs1042059 and rs11591377, and their possible effect on leukaemia risk.

The authors gathered case-control studies, large genome scans, and lab studies of how the gene works. Some reported that these variants raised leukaemia risk, perhaps by changing gene activity and growth signals. Other studies, in other populations, found no such link. The review judges the evidence inconclusive overall. It calls for larger population studies and clearer work on the mechanism. If confirmed, the variants could help refine risk checks and personal treatment choices in future.
pmc-13282864:
Can extra calcium help control blood pressure after menopause? Ahmed Farouk Alaarag and fellow clinicians tested that idea in 2026. The study enrolled women who had both low blood calcium and hypertension. Low calcium after menopause may raise blood pressure by affecting blood vessel tone.

A total of 300 women received calcium carbonate at 1,000 mg per day plus usual blood pressure drugs. Staff measured blood pressure and calcium at the start and after three months. Women whose calcium returned to normal showed better blood pressure control. More of them reached target levels. The authors suggest that fixing low calcium may aid standard treatment.
pmc-13283164:
An adult bleeding-risk score for brain vessel tangles falters in children, Frankfurt records analyzed by Sepide Kashefiolasl show in 2026. Such tangles are a top cause of brain bleeding in young patients. The VALE score was built for adults, so its value in children was unknown.

Hospital records in Frankfurt covered 52 patients aged 18 years or younger from 2005 to 2023. A total of 31 patients arrived with bleeding at first care. Only one score part, a vein bulge near the tangle, stayed linked to bleeding after full adjustment. The full score sorted risk poorly in children by standard tests. The authors advise against direct use of the adult score for child patients.
pmc-13283264:
Nanoparticles that kill germs by fresh routes headline Akmal Zubair's 2026 survey of superbug countermeasures. Germs that resist many drugs are a rising global health threat. Few new antibiotics are emerging, and old drugs keep losing strength.

The review explains how bacteria resist drugs, from pumping drugs out to shielding targets. Tiny particles can kill germs by new routes or carry drugs past defenses. Metal, organic, carbon-based, and hybrid particles all showed strong germ killing. Pairing particles with plant compounds is also under active study in the field. The authors weigh safety and scale-up needs for clinical use. Nano tools may revive options against hard infections.
pmc-13283364:
Five bedside factors combine into the Base-C score for spotting collapsed-lung treatment failure, Xiangli Shao's hospital team reports in 2026. Collapsed lung from air leaks often fails non-surgical care. Early spotting of high-risk patients can speed the right intervention.

Records came from two large hospitals for score building and testing. The main cohort held 1,378 patients, and the check cohort held 506 patients. Five factors formed the Base-C score: air blisters, age, smoking, emphysema, and collapse size. The score sorted failure risk well in both cohorts by standard tests. Fit checks also looked good in the validation work. The tool can help tailor care plans early.
pmc-13284364:
Zhengkai Yang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a blood protein can flag complex heart artery disease before invasive imaging. The SYNTAX score grades how complex narrowed coronary anatomy is, yet it needs a catheter procedure. The protein LRG1 rises with inflammation and vessel injury. The team mined public gene datasets, then measured LRG1 in 138 patients with confirmed coronary disease at one centre.

Gene data showed LRG1 overexpressed in heart attack patients, and blood levels ran higher in heart attack cases than in stable cases. Patients with high complexity scores carried far higher LRG1 levels than those with low scores. Feature selection kept LRG1 and LDL cholesterol as independent predictors, and a combined chart model sorted complex anatomy with moderate accuracy.
pmc-13284564:
Chang Hyun Kim and Sang Hyub Lee presented in 2026 a hard-to-diagnose lymphoma case that surfaced mainly in the gut. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a mature T-cell cancer marked by the CD30 protein. The ALK-negative systemic form usually strikes older adults and behaves aggressively, and gut-dominant disease is rare. Their patient had a past slow-growing B-cell skin lymphoma and arrived with long, intermittent fever and whole-body symptoms.

Standard scans, a PET-CT, and a bone marrow test all failed to pin the cause. New gut symptoms and falling albumin pushed the team to scope the stomach, which revealed several ulcerated, fungus-like growths. Tissue study showed large abnormal lymphoid cells with strong CD30, no ALK, fast growth markers, and a clonal T-cell signature. Treatment with a targeted antibody drug plus chemotherapy eased the fevers.
pmc-13285364:
Forecasting who will still hurt a year after knee replacement stays hard, even for smart algorithms, Anni Rajamäki and co-authors show in a 2026 cohort study. Between ten and twenty percent of patients end up unhappy after surgery, so a good forecast could steer counseling and spare needless operations. The team fed 751 patient traits into boosted-tree models for 11,755 patients.

About seven percent still had lasting pain at one year. Model accuracy landed in the poor range for pain and for the paired score outcomes. Low starting knee scores, younger age, and higher body weight ranked among the top signals. The authors conclude pain after this surgery resists prediction with current data.
pmc-13285564:
A helpful fungus may rein in the anthracnose blight that rots crops worldwide, Rendra Adhitya and co-authors review in a 2026 article. Colletotrichum fungi hit over three thousand plant kinds and swap between quiet and killing growth phases, which foils control. Chemical sprays bring resistance, pollution, and food safety worries.

Lab, greenhouse, field, and storage trials show Trichoderma can curb the blight, best under controlled terms. Weather, strain pick, product shelf life, and spray style all sway results in the works surveyed here. The authors urge gene-wide studies, strain tuning, and better formulas so farm results hold steady, letting growers cut chemical use while crops resist disease better.
pmc-13286164:
Julia Döge and colleagues link hearing loss with planning skill in a 2026 population cohort study from Mainz, Germany. Straining to hear may drain the mental budget that planning draws on, but proof on single thinking skills has stayed scarce. Volunteers took tone tests, a speech-in-noise test, and a tower puzzle that grades how well a person plans ahead.

Records held 4,458 adults aged 40 to 80 with full hearing and puzzle data. People with measured hearing loss scored lower on planning overall, though loss alone did not push them into the clinical danger zone. Stronger planners, in turn, showed lower odds of hearing loss and picked speech out of noise more cleanly. The two-way pattern fits the idea that hearing effort taxes shared brain resources, and the authors call for long-term studies to sort cause from effect.
pmc-13286764:
Milda Mikalonytė and a large team report two patients whose rare T-cell lymphoma involved the brain and spinal cord, treated with a targeted drug called alectinib. Published in 2026, the cases address a grim corner of lymphoma care: this ALK-positive type usually responds well, yet disease in the central nervous system has no standard treatment and poor outcomes.

An 18-year-old man relapsed in the nervous system after chemotherapy and a stem cell transplant. Alectinib plus chemotherapy delivered into the spinal fluid, followed by a donor transplant, kept him in remission for more than six years. A 31-year-old woman whose disease began in the nervous system also reached remission and stayed there for twenty months on maintenance treatment.
pmc-13286864:
M Kodeeswaran and a multinational team describe repairing a giant torn artery bulge inside the skull in their 2026 case report. The patient, a 48-year-old woman, endured two months of dull left-sided headache, then a week of blurred vision and a weakening right arm. Imaging revealed a dissecting pseudoaneurysm of the left internal carotid artery just above its bony canal, pressing on nearby brain with mild midline shift.

Surgeons reached the lesion through the leg artery rather than open surgery. A flow-diverting stent bridged the diseased stretch from the carotid into the middle cerebral artery, and soft platinum coils packed the sac to spur clotting. Final angiography showed the bulge nearly shut out of circulation while the parent artery and its branches stayed open. The report pairs the case with a literature review favoring this combined route for high-risk lesions.
pmc-13287164:
Luísa dos Santos Conceição and co-authors reviewed fifteen years of work in 2026 on quixabeira, a thorny medicinal tree known to rural communities in Brazil. Their aim was to gather what is known about each plant part and where useful products or treatments might realistically come from.

Leaf extracts were studied most, often made with methanol or ethanol, and showed antioxidant and microbe-fighting activity in laboratory tests. Fruit work is thinner, though pigments and flavonoids were measured. Local uses span food, medicine, animal care, and building. The reviewers say safety and dosing work is still missing, so claimed benefits should be treated as early leads awaiting stronger checks.
pmc-13287464:
Faxin Zhou and colleagues recorded brain activity in 2026 from electrodes placed inside the skulls of 19 people watching a short film in several languages. The aim was to see how the frontal cortex handles sound and picture together during lifelike viewing, rather than in stripped-down lab tasks.

A clear gradient appeared: lower frontal areas leaned toward sound, upper areas toward vision. That layout shifted as film scenes changed, suggesting flexible sharing of work. Behaviour ratings pointed to the frontal cortex as the main site sorting out which sense leads. The authors read the pattern as a flexible system that builds one story from two input streams.
pmc-13287564:
Dong Won Kwack and Dong Wook Kim piloted slow-release melatonin in 2026 in adults who live with both epilepsy and insomnia. Thirty-four patients enrolled between March 2024 and February 2025, and 25 finished twelve weeks of nightly tablets. Sleep and mood scales were taken before and after.

Sleep scores improved clearly over the twelve weeks. Depression scores fell by a smaller but real margin. Seizure patterns did not change, and nobody stopped the tablets because seizures worsened. Most finishers had focal seizures. The authors present the hormone tablet as a candidate add-on for sleep and mood in epilepsy, while noting the small, uncontrolled design.
pmc-13288864:
Jae-Woo Song, Sunhee Yoon, Sunghoon Jung, and Wang-Hee Lee refresh climate data for species models in 2026. Many forecasts still use old climate averages. Those averages run from 1961 to 1990. The team built a global database for 1992 to 2021. It was shaped for the CLIMEX system.

Three species were modeled as a test. Both CLIMEX and MaxEnt were used. Old and new baselines were compared. Overall skill barely moved. Broad niche overlap barely moved either. Local fit shifted clearly in places. Occurrence chances shifted there too. Matching climate years to sighting years should cut error. Pest risk and biosecurity work stand to gain.
pmc-13289064:
Leopold Hentschel and colleagues study strain on family caregivers in Germany. Their 2026 study deals with home palliative care. One clinic team ran the study. Recruitment ran from April 2021 to August 2022. The team logged illness and home facts.

Of 250 patients screened, 152 pairs joined. Low mood topped the mark in 31 percent of caregivers. Worry topped it in 33 percent. Broad distress hit 82 percent of them. More care hours per day tied to low mood. COVID strain also tied to low mood. Oddly, COVID strain tied to less worry. The models left most strain unexplained.
pmc-13289364:
Junho Kang, Jinhyeon An, and Jung Kyoon Choi built a 2026 atlas comparing immune side effects of cancer checkpoint drugs with chronic inflammatory diseases. Both can look alike in symptoms and treatment, yet their cell-level drivers may differ. The team merged gene data from millions of cells to map where the two kinds of inflammation truly diverge.

The compendium held over 4.3 million cells from 1137 samples plus spatial maps and blood data before and after treatment. Side-effect tissues showed a distinct mix rich in certain phagocytes, dendritic cells, and chemical signals, plus special regulatory and tired T cells in tight niches. Severe side effects tied to higher CXCL10 signaling after treatment and to a specific HLA type in carriers.
pmc-13289464:
Caroline Cohrdes and coauthors present a 2026 population study on mental paths linking hard life events to later well-being in young adults. Potentially traumatic events include not only classic trauma but also social harms such as exclusion and discrimination. The authors test shared mental processes that cut across diagnoses, rather than one disorder at a time.

Data covered 3,051 emerging adults in a population sample, modeled with structural equations for indirect links. Three broad process groups emerged: thought-focused, emotion-focused, and social-focused paths between events and outcomes. Emotion-focused paths carried the largest share of indirect links overall. Social exclusion showed the strongest and steadiest ties to mental health, and models explained inner distress better than outer behavior or positive health.
pmc-13289764:
Rapeepong Suphanchaimat headed a 2026 study on whether public insurance cuts out-of-pocket costs for mental health care among migrants who cross borders into Thailand. Migrant insurance schemes exist, yet mental health care is not clearly listed as covered, and cost evidence was scarce. Routine service data from public hospitals nationwide covered 2018 to 2022 for the analysis.

A total of 4,559 patients made 13,744 visits, and 84.1 percent were uninsured at care. Mean spending per visit was 449 Baht, with a very wide range up to over one hundred thousand Baht as reported. A two-part model with machine learning found insurance cut the chance of any payment by about half. Mean cost per visit also ran lower for insured patients.
pmc-13290164:
Reddit talk during the 2022 mpox outbreak is analyzed by Xi Ning Luo and colleagues in a 2026 observational study. Health emergencies tend to stir uncertainty, stigma, and rumor online, and the authors wanted to see how sentiment, topics, and engagement interacted on one platform.

They gathered 1,169 posts and 6,571 comments from four mpox subreddits and sorted them with sentiment analysis and topic modeling into nine themes. Most posts were neutral in tone, about a third negative, and a smaller share positive. Negative posts drew higher engagement scores than positive ones, and comments tended to echo the tone of the post they answered. Luo and colleagues say communicators should expect emotional narratives to spread fastest and plan responses accordingly.
pmc-13290564:
Acupuncture alongside IVF may lift pregnancy rates for women with diminished ovarian reserve, Liangliang Xu and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Low egg supply is a stubborn cause of infertility, and earlier trials of needling disagreed.

Searching eight databases, the team pooled 11 randomized trials covering 885 women undergoing IVF or ICSI. The pooled results favored acupuncture: clinical pregnancy (risk difference 0.25), live birth (0.22), and implantation (0.30) all ran higher with treatment, with more eggs retrieved and more top-quality embryos too. Subgroup checks held up, but the graded certainty of evidence ranged only from very low to moderate. Xu and colleagues call the signal promising and ask for stricter trials to confirm it.
pmc-13290864:
Alzheimer's blood markers track brain shrinkage and thinking problems inside Parkinson's disease, Eleonora Fiorenzato and colleagues report in a biomarker study from 2026. Alzheimer co-pathology may speed decline in Parkinson's, and cheap plasma tests now allow staging it, but their meaning for Parkinson's types was unclear.

Fifty-eight Parkinson's patients across the cognitive spectrum and 76 dementia-free older adults gave blood, MRI scans, and cognitive testing. The Alzheimer markers p-tau217 and the amyloid ratio beat the nerve-damage and inflammation markers: higher p-tau217 meant more Alzheimer-like MRI change and worse cognition in both groups. In Parkinson's it also mapped onto memory and executive problems, and mood symptoms tracked the Alzheimer markers too. Fiorenzato and colleagues back p-tau217 especially for sorting Parkinson's patients by biology.
pmc-13290964:
Junjie Cao leads a 2026 landscape study of clinical trials testing immune checkpoint inhibitors for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of primary liver cancer. Rather than testing a drug, the team mapped how this research area is organized around the world.

Four international trial databases were searched through February 14, 2026, leaving 132 trials that met the study rules. China accounted for 95 trials and the United States for 16, while most work targeted PD-1 or PD-L1 and few trials targeted CTLA-4. Phase II work was most common, with 59 trials listed. Very few results had been published, so the authors urge better reporting and wider collaboration.
pmc-13291064:
Sudarshan Choudhary, Rahul Gurpude, and Amrut Mulay form magnesium skull plates with heat assistance in a 2026 study. AZ31B magnesium alloy is light and body-friendly, suiting cranial implants. Its weakness is poor shaping at room temperature. The team used single point incremental forming, where a tool presses sheet metal step by step along a programmed path. Gentle heating to four hundred degrees let the perforated sheet reach implant depth.

Trials settled on a twelve-millimeter tool and holes of three and a half millimeters as the best pairing. That pairing gave the most even shaping and the smoothest surface. A zigzag tool path at a set feed rate and fine step depth then formed a cranial plate with high precision. Microscope and hardness checks tracked how the metal's inner structure changed. Simulations modeled stress and strain per setting. The authors offer the recipe for custom, patient-matched skull implants.
pmc-13291264:
Trees that learn can stay small and clear. Sabino Francesco Roselli and Eibe Frank test best-possible model trees in a 2026 study. Normal tree methods grow greedily, split by split. Each split looks good alone but may miss the best whole tree.

Model trees put math formulas in their leaves. Optimal versions were built with mixed integer planning. Leaves held linear support vector machines. Tests used standard benchmark data sets. Rivals included greedy trees, forests, and support machines. Optimal trees matched strong accuracy with tiny size. Slanted splits boosted accuracy but blurred clarity. The trade-off between clear and sharp is made plain.
pmc-13291564:
Virtual reality may make colon checks calmer and less painful. Yijie Sun leads a 2026 randomized trial of VR during colonoscopy. Adults aged 18 to 70 took part without sedation. Pain and anxiety are common barriers to screening.

Patients were split into VR and control groups. Pain, anxiety, and vital signs were tracked live. VR users felt less pain and less anxiety. Their heart rate and blood pressure also ran lower. Procedure time and success matched the control group. More VR users would accept a future colon check. That gain could lift screening rates over time. Comfort care need not slow the procedure down.
pmc-13291764:
Crone and co-authors map the worldwide use of gut stimulating drugs in intensive care in this 2026 PATIENCE study. Feeding intolerance is common in critically ill patients, and prokinetic agents are given to move the gut along. Evidence for them is thin, so practice varies. The team followed newly admitted patients in 56 intensive care units across 11 countries.

Among 1440 patients, 187 received a prokinetic agent during their stay, roughly one patient in eight. Metoclopramide was the drug used most often. Patients who had undergone abdominal surgery before were more likely to receive one. Use of these drugs came with a higher hazard of serious adverse events and fewer days alive out of intensive care and hospital, though not with higher 90 day mortality. Crone presents the figures as a baseline for future trials.
pmc-13292264:
Karim Qayumi and a large team evaluate a 2026 digital medical school built for Afghan women shut out of university classrooms. The Canadian Virtual Medical University Initiative delivers an online, competency-based curriculum built around five entrustable professional activities across body systems. Lectures came through Lecturio, and CyberPatient supplied simulated clinical practice.

Ninety-two former Afghan medical students with strong English and reliable internet joined the first term, studying from November 2024 to July 2025. Level I students gained 52 to 58 points on knowledge tests across every system taught, with strong statistical significance. Level II students also improved in knowledge and in virtual clinical exam performance. The authors present the model as a workable lifeline where campuses, faculty, and women's access have collapsed.
pmc-13292464:
Ellainy Maria Conceição Silva and co-authors use a 2026 shellfish survey to test whether Maranhão Island's bivalves carry Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite behind toxoplasmosis. Oysters, mussels, and clams came from natural mangrove beds around four island municipalities through 2022, in both rainy and dry seasons. Gill tissue pools underwent DNA extraction and gene testing targeting SAG1, with deeper marker panels for positives.

Three mussel pools, 1.8 percent of the sixty tested, came back positive, all from rainy-season collections in Raposa and São José de Ribamar. Sequence matching confirmed 98 to 100 percent similarity with known Toxoplasma sequences, though extra markers failed to amplify, limiting genotype claims. Tree analysis grouped the finds with classical genotype references. The authors recommend monitoring shellfish grounds as a food safety measure.
pmc-13292564:
Zhengyu Fan and co-authors compare flavor chemistry across three duck breeds after boiling, in a 2026 metabolomics study. Cherry Valley, Jinling White, and Liancheng White ducks were cooked in water, and meat plus broth were profiled. Untargeted metabolomics hunted the small molecules behind breed flavor differences. Boiling itself reshaped the chemistry as compounds formed and migrated. Jinling White sat between the other two on key flavor compounds.

Its middling levels of cysteine, a thiazole, furaneol, and several dipeptides may explain a balanced, appealing taste. Pathway analysis pointed to amino acid metabolism, nucleotide breakdown, fat metabolism, and carbohydrate breakdown as the engines of difference. Heat-driven reactions like Maillard chemistry and lipid oxidation built the final profiles. The authors say metabolomics can dissect how breed and cooking jointly create flavor. Breeders and processors could use such maps to target preferred tastes. The study centers on boiled duck, a common preparation.
pmc-13292664:
Lara Hamzeh Hamzeh and a large team pool a 2026 meta-analysis on magnetic brain stimulation for freezing of gait, the sudden stepping stall that makes Parkinson's patients fall. Searching four databases through January 2026 under PRISMA 2020 rules, they kept randomized trials only. The main outcome was freezing severity on the standard questionnaire.

Twelve trials with 293 participants qualified. Stimulation improved freezing scores by a standardized mean difference of 0.97 in the pooled estimate, a solid effect. Motor ratings, Timed Up and Go times, walking speed, stride length, and turning measures all improved too, while cadence alone stayed flat. No serious adverse events appeared in any trial. The authors call the therapy a safe, promising add-on for gait problems that resist drugs, while asking for bigger trials with shared protocols.
pmc-13292764: Penelope Banchi and co-authors issued this brief correction in 2026 to their review on early-life gut microbes in dogs and cats. The notice fixes one label in Figure 1 and states that the review itself has been updated. The figure had shown weaning for puppies and kittens with a wrong age note, and the correct wording is more than 2 months of age. No findings or advice in the review change. Readers who need the timeline for feeding and weaning should use the corrected figure.
pmc-13293364:
Ericka Stoor-Burning leads a 2026 Army study comparing three prototype sensor suits that record battlefield casualty care without adding hands-on work. Medics in combat zones have little time to chart care, so passive recording could fill the gap.

Testing ran in three stages: bench review, practice use, and a full simulation event under varied lighting. All three suits passed basic checks, and simpler layouts scored best on capturing and exporting raw data. In practice runs, usability scores ran from 60 to 85 out of 100, a spread the authors report. Display lag for vital signs raised trust concerns among users.
pmc-13293464:
Muzafar Riyaz and co-authors compare, in a 2026 field study, insect pollinators in sprayed apple orchards and nearby unsprayed graveyards in Shopian, Kashmir. Heavy spray schedules may do more than poison insects directly; they may also warp how insects choose flowers.

Eight orchards held far fewer insects and species than paired graveyards, with hoverflies and lone bees hit hardest. Visiting networks in orchards grew sparser and less nested, and insects fed on fewer flower types. One common flower drew most visits during peak spraying, acting as a trap with no clean option nearby. Long-tongued insects fell sharply, flattening the pollinator mix.
pmc-13293564:
Arun Dahil and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, a planned review of clot complications from cardiac myxoma, the most common benign heart tumor. Though benign, these tumors can shed fragments that cause stroke, heart attack, or limb and organ damage.

The review will search six databases for large case series, cohort studies, and registries with confirmed tumors. Pairs of reviewers will screen and extract data, with bias checked by standard tools. Planned outputs cover how often clots occur, where they land, how patients present, and how care is managed. The protocol aims to fill a gap in pooled knowledge; no results are given yet.
pmc-13293664:
Shireen Dogar and colleagues combine, in a 2026 paper, a literature review and hospital cohort on wrist tissue biopsy as an early test for heart amyloidosis. A wrist operation for carpal tunnel release offers a chance to spot the protein buildup before heart failure starts.

The review of 22 studies from 2017 to 2025 found amyloid in 10% to 30% of wrist specimens, a range the authors report. At their center, 89 patients had biopsy during release surgery from 2021 to 2025, over half of them African American. No specimen showed amyloid on staining. Better patient picking and sampling rules are needed, the authors conclude.
pmc-13293764:
Jiahui Chen and colleagues decode what makes yeast protein smell the way it does, in a 2026 flavor chemistry study. Yeast protein is a sustainable, high-quality protein source, but wider use in foods depends on understanding and improving its flavor. The team combined trained sensory panels with advanced gas analysis, using three extraction methods to capture the full range of scent compounds.

Panelists rated roasted, sour, sweet, and almond-like notes as dominant. The combined extraction approach found 104 odor-active compounds, and rebuilding the scent from parts reproduced the original with ninety percent similarity. Leaving compounds out one at a time confirmed eleven as the true drivers, including benzaldehyde and several fatty acids. The framework gives makers a way to check flavor quality and guide product development for yeast-based foods.
pmc-13294064:
Zongxin Ling and coauthors compare gut microbes and inflammation in older adults with high blood pressure, with and without memory-type mild cognitive impairment, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Groups held 52 healthy controls, 83 hypertensive adults with normal cognition, and 70 hypertensive adults with impairment. Stool sequencing and a 27-marker blood panel were combined.

The impaired group showed richer but clearly separate gut communities, with fewer short-chain fatty acid makers like Roseburia and Faecalibacterium and more opportunistic genera. Inflammatory signals including IL-6 and IL-8 ran higher. Blautia levels tracked with lower inflammation and better cognition, while pathobiont levels tracked the opposite way.
pmc-13294164:
Meriem El Karoui, Ignacio Madrid, and Sylvie Méléard model a bacterial survival trade-off in a 2026 math study. Under low antibiotic stress, E. coli cells can randomly switch on the SOS response, which helps them endure damage but slows division. Their two-type, age-structured model splits cells into fast but fragile growers and slow but tolerant responders, in steady and pulsing stress.
